aspendos.t: Aspendos, a wealthy Pamphylian city on the Eurymedon river, near which Athens defeated Persia and later the Romans built a famous theatre.
aspendos.o: Aspendos rose on a hill by the Eurymedon river, a few kilometres from the sea, in the 7th century BCE. Its people claimed descent from settlers from Argos, but its coins were inscribed in the local Pamphylian Greek dialect with the name Estwediiys.
aspendos.r: The city prospered from horse breeding, farming and salt and river trade, and minted silver coins. Around 466 BCE the Athenian general Cimon defeated a Persian fleet and army near the Eurymedon. In 333 BCE Aspendos submitted to Alexander, who demanded tribute and horses after it reneged on terms.
aspendos.e: Aspendos passed under Seleucid and Pergamene influence, then Roman rule, joining the province of Galatia in 25 BCE. Its theatre, built in the 2nd century CE, is one of the best preserved from antiquity.

ayyubid-emirate-of-mayyafariqin.t: The Ayyubid principality of Diyar Bakr, whose last prince died resisting the Mongols after a long siege in 1260.
ayyubid-emirate-of-mayyafariqin.o: Saladin took Mayyafariqin in 1185 from the Shah-Armens' sphere and gave it to his brother al-Adil, whose son al-Awhad Ayyub ruled it and in 1207 took Ahlat. It became a hereditary Ayyubid principality in the Jazira.
ayyubid-emirate-of-mayyafariqin.r: The principality passed to al-Ashraf Musa and then to al-Muzaffar Ghazi, sons of al-Adil, and then to Ghazi's son al-Kamil Muhammad. Its rulers controlled the old Marwanid capital, rich farmland north of the Tigris and roads to Ahlat. They faced the Khwarazmians, the Sultanate of Rum and finally the Mongols. Al-Kamil Muhammad defied Hulagu.
ayyubid-emirate-of-mayyafariqin.e: Mongol forces besieged Mayyafariqin from 1259; in 1260 the city fell after famine, al-Kamil Muhammad was killed and his head was paraded in Syrian cities.

archbishopric-of-riga.t: Ecclesiastical principality that led the Christian conquest of Livonia and governed much of Latvia for nearly four centuries.
archbishopric-of-riga.o: The missionary Meinhard became bishop of the Livs at Üxküll in 1186. His successor Albert of Buxhoeveden founded Riga in 1201 and moved the see there, directing the crusade with the Livonian Brothers of the Sword. In 1255 Riga was raised to an archbishopric under Albert Suerbeer, with authority over the bishoprics of Livonia and Prussia.
archbishopric-of-riga.r: The archbishops were princes of the Holy Roman Empire, ruling lands along the Daugava and Gauja through vassals and castles such as Turaida and Kokenhusen. Their rule was marked by long conflicts with the Livonian Order and with the citizens of Riga over control of the city. The cathedral chapter and vassals sat in the Livonian diets.
archbishopric-of-riga.e: The Reformation reached Riga in the 1520s, weakening the archbishops. During the Livonian War the last archbishop, Wilhelm of Brandenburg, placed his lands under Polish-Lithuanian protection, and in 1561-1562 they were secularised and incorporated into the Duchy of Livonia under Sigismund II Augustus.

ancient-shu.t: The early kingdom of the Sichuan basin, heir to the astonishing bronze culture of Sanxingdui, conquered by Qin in 316 BCE.
ancient-shu.o: Shu emerged in the Chengdu plain from a long local tradition: the Sanxingdui culture, with its giant bronze masks and standing figure, and the later Jinsha site in Chengdu. Later legends name a series of kings, Cancong, Yufu and Duyu, followed by the Kaiming dynasty, but these accounts were written centuries afterwards.
ancient-shu.r: Shu developed largely independently of the Zhou states, and its bronze art, sun worship and burial customs, including boat-shaped coffins, differ sharply from those of northern China. Under the Kaiming kings it was centred on Chengdu and was rich in rice, salt and copper. It had no widely used script; the so-called Ba-Shu signs remain undeciphered.
ancient-shu.e: Quarrels between Shu and the neighbouring State of Ba gave the State of Qin a pretext; in 316 BCE the Qin general Sima Cuo conquered Shu. Qin settled colonists there, and the governor Li Bing built the Dujiangyan irrigation system, making Sichuan the granary that fuelled Qin's unification of China.

areopagus-of-eastern-continental-greece.t: Regional revolutionary government of eastern mainland Greece in 1821-1822, set up at Salona under Theodoros Negris.
areopagus-of-eastern-continental-greece.o: Eastern mainland Greece, including Attica, Boeotia, Phocis and Locris, joined the revolution in 1821. In November 1821 an assembly of local representatives met at Salona (Amfissa) and, under the guidance of the Phanariot diplomat Theodoros Negris, adopted a legal charter and created a governing council named after the ancient Athenian Areopagus.
areopagus-of-eastern-continental-greece.r: The Areopagus was made up of local notables and was meant to run the administration, justice and war effort in the region. It struggled to control powerful armed chieftains, above all Odysseas Androutsos, with whom it was in open conflict. Its authority over the scattered and contested territory was limited.
areopagus-of-eastern-continental-greece.e: After the First National Assembly at Epidaurus created the First Hellenic Republic in January 1822, the regional bodies were subordinated to central government. The Areopagus continued for a time but lost its role during 1822 and 1823.

akusha-dargo-union.t: A powerful union of self-governing Dargin communities in central Dagestan, led by the qadi of Akusha, which long resisted both khans and Russia.
akusha-dargo-union.o: The Dargin highlands of central Dagestan were home to free communities, called jamaats, that governed themselves without princes. By the 17th century the largest of them formed a union around the village of Akusha, whose qadi, a religious judge, served as its leading authority.
akusha-dargo-union.r: The union was a confederation of village communities with their own assemblies and customary law, coordinated by the qadi and councils of elders. It could field several thousand warriors and was among the strongest forces in Dagestan. Its people farmed terraced fields, herded sheep and were known for metalworking in villages such as Kubachi nearby.
akusha-dargo-union.e: General Yermolov defeated the Akusha forces at Levashi in 1819 and imposed Russian authority. The union was finally incorporated into the Russian Empire in 1844 amid the wars of the Caucasian Imamate.

andecavi.t: Gallic people of Anjou whose leader Dumnacus fought one of the last campaigns against Rome in 51 BCE.
andecavi.o: The Andecavi, called Andes by Caesar, lived on the lower Loire around Angers. Caesar quartered legions among them in 57 BCE and records that they joined the revolt of 52 BCE.
andecavi.r: Little is known of their institutions beyond their war leaders.
andecavi.e: In 51 BCE Dumnacus besieged the pro-Roman Pictones in Lemonum, but was defeated by Caesar's legate Gaius Fabius and fled. Under Rome their chief town was Juliomagus, later called Andecavi, the origin of Angers and of the name Anjou.

archchancellors-electorate.t: State created for Karl Theodor von Dalberg, the last Archbishop of Mainz, to keep the imperial archchancellor's office alive.
archchancellors-electorate.o: When the left bank of the Rhine passed to France, the Electorate of Mainz lost its capital. The Imperial Recess of 1803 kept its archbishop, Karl Theodor von Dalberg, as elector and archchancellor of the Empire, and gave him the Principality of Aschaffenburg, Regensburg and the County of Wetzlar, with the archiepiscopal seat moved to Regensburg.
archchancellors-electorate.r: Dalberg was an Enlightenment churchman who governed from Regensburg, seat of the Perpetual Imperial Diet. His state was scattered and Catholic, with Aschaffenburg as its richest part. He cultivated Napoleon, praising him as a new Charlemagne, and in 1806 became Prince-Primate of the Confederation of the Rhine, adding Frankfurt to his lands.
archchancellors-electorate.e: In 1810 Dalberg ceded Regensburg to the Kingdom of Bavaria and in exchange received Hanau and Fulda, creating the Grand Duchy of Frankfurt. Dalberg remained its ruler until 1813, and Regensburg has belonged to Bavaria ever since.

anconine-republic.t: A short-lived French-backed republic in the Adriatic port of Ancona, carved from the Papal States in 1797 and merged into the Roman Republic.
anconine-republic.o: French troops occupied Ancona, the main Adriatic port of the Papal States, in February 1797, and the Treaty of Tolentino left them in control of it. In November 1797 local patriots, with French encouragement, proclaimed the Anconine Republic, with jurisdiction over Ancona and nearby towns of the Marche.
anconine-republic.r: The republic was governed by a provisional administration of local Jacobins under French military control. It abolished the old papal institutions, freed the city's Jews from the ghetto restrictions and adopted French-style laws and symbols. It also served as a base for French plans against the rest of the Papal States.
anconine-republic.e: When French troops occupied Rome and created the Roman Republic (1798–1799) in February 1798, the Anconine Republic was absorbed into it in March 1798.

assaka.t: The only mahajanapada south of the Vindhya mountains, an early kingdom on the Godavari river in the northern Deccan.
assaka.o: Assaka, Ashmaka in Sanskrit, is named in Buddhist lists of the sixteen great states and by the grammarian Panini. It lay on the Godavari river, with its capital at Potali or Potana, often identified with Bodhan in modern Telangana. Its origins are obscure, and later tradition linked its kings to the Ikshvaku line.
assaka.r: Little is known of its government. The Sutta Nipata tells of the Brahmin teacher Bavari, who lived on the Godavari in the Assaka country and sent his pupils north to meet the Buddha, which shows the kingdom's links along the southern trade route, the Dakshinapatha, to the Ganges valley. Its neighbour Mulaka lay around Pratishthana.
assaka.e: Assaka appears to have come under the influence of the Kingdom of Avanti and was later absorbed into the Nanda and Maurya empires. After the Mauryas its region formed part of the heartland of the Satavahana dynasty.

astures.t: The peoples of Asturias and León, last in Iberia to fall to Rome in 19 BCE, whose land became the empire's great gold-mining district.
astures.o: The Astures occupied the lands between the Cantabrian coast and the Douro, in modern Asturias, León and northern Zamora, from about the 4th century BCE. Romans divided them into the Transmontani north of the mountains and the Augustani on the plateau to the south.
astures.r: They lived in castros, fortified hilltop villages of round stone houses, in many independent communities grouped by kinship. Herding, farming and metalworking supported them, and their mountains held rich gold deposits. Their main stronghold on the plain was Lancia, near León. They spoke a Celtic language.
astures.e: The Astures fought alongside the Cantabri in Augustus' Cantabrian Wars of 29 to 19 BCE. After conquest Rome founded Asturica Augusta (Astorga) and exploited the gold of Las Médulas on a vast scale. Their name survives in Asturias and in the later Kingdom of Asturias.

argungu-emirate.t: The successor of the Hausa Kingdom of Kebbi, which resisted the Sokoto Caliphate for most of the 19th century from its fortified capital at Argungu.
argungu-emirate.o: The Kingdom of Kebbi lost its capital, Birnin Kebbi, to Fulani jihadists in 1805, but its rulers kept fighting from the marshes and towns to the north. Around 1831 they made Argungu, on the Sokoto river, their base, and from there the Kebbawa continued the war against the Gwandu Emirate and Sokoto.
argungu-emirate.r: Argungu was a fortified Hausa state that kept old Kebbi titles and institutions. Its rulers were Muslims who rejected the political claims of the caliphate, and they allied with other Hausa refugees in Gobir and Maradi. The wars brought frequent raids and counter-raids, interrupted by truces, and the emirate's people farmed and fished in the river valley.
argungu-emirate.e: British forces occupied Argungu in 1902, and it became an emirate of the Protectorate of Northern Nigeria. Its emir still reigns, and the town is famous for the Argungu Fishing Festival, held annually since the 1930s.

alba-longa.t: Legendary mother city of the Latins in the Alban Hills, remembered by the Romans as the home of Romulus and Remus and the seat of the Latin festival.
alba-longa.o: Roman tradition held that Ascanius, son of the Trojan hero Aeneas, founded Alba Longa about thirty years after Lavinium, and placed its foundation in the 12th century BCE. Archaeology shows Iron Age villages and cemeteries around the Alban Lake and Monte Cavo from about 1000 BCE, but no single city has been firmly identified.
alba-longa.r: The Romans described a line of Alban kings, from Silvius to Numitor and his usurping brother Amulius, but these are legendary. What is more secure is the role of the Alban Hills as a religious centre for the Latin peoples: the sanctuary of Jupiter Latiaris on Monte Cavo hosted the Feriae Latinae, a shared festival that Rome kept celebrating long after Alba disappeared.
alba-longa.e: According to Livy, Rome under Tullus Hostilius defeated Alba after the duel of the Horatii and Curiatii in the mid-7th century BCE, razed the city and moved its people to the Caelian Hill. Leading Roman families such as the Julii claimed Alban descent, and the Latin League inherited its religious role.

antes.t: An early Slavic people between the Dniester and the Dnieper, known from Byzantine writers as raiders and allies of the 6th-century empire.
antes.o: The Antes appear in the 6th century in Procopius and Jordanes, who describe them as a people related to the Sclaveni living east of the Dniester. Archaeologists usually connect them with the Penkovka culture. Jordanes also tells how an Antian leader named Boz was killed by the Goths, but the story is hard to date.
antes.r: Procopius says the Antes were not ruled by one man but lived in a kind of democracy, deciding matters in common, and worshipped a god of lightning as lord of all. They farmed, kept livestock and lived in scattered villages. From the 530s they raided the Balkans, but Justinian also hired them as allies to guard the Danube.
antes.e: The Avars attacked them in the 560s, and an Avar expedition sent against them in 602 is the last time the Antes are mentioned. Their people were absorbed into the East Slavic tribes of later centuries, while the title Anticus lingered for a time in the Byzantine emperor's style.

argentine-republic.t: The republic reunited under Buenos Aires in 1861, which became one of the world's richest countries by 1900 before a century of political turmoil.
argentine-republic.o: After Bartolomé Mitre's victory at Pavón in 1861 over the Argentine Confederation, Buenos Aires and the provinces were reunited under the Constitution of 1853, as amended in 1860, which adopted the name Argentine Republic. Mitre became president in 1862.
argentine-republic.r: Mitre, Domingo Sarmiento and Nicolás Avellaneda built national institutions and schools. Argentina fought Paraguay from 1865 to 1870, and Julio Argentino Roca's Conquest of the Desert seized the pampas and Patagonia. Mass immigration from Italy and Spain and exports of beef and wheat made it among the world's richest countries by 1914. A military coup in 1930 began decades of instability. Juan Perón led a powerful labour-based movement from 1946.
argentine-republic.e: The dictatorship of 1976 to 1983 killed thousands in the Dirty War and lost the Falklands War. Democracy returned in 1983 under Raúl Alfonsín. Repeated economic crises, including a default in 2001, followed, and Javier Milei was elected in 2023.

aram-zobah.t: Aram-Zobah, an Aramaean kingdom of the 10th century BCE, the main rival of King David in the Bible.
aram-zobah.o: Zobah was an Aramaean kingdom probably centred on the Beqaa valley and the region north of Damascus. It is known almost entirely from the Hebrew Bible, which describes its king Hadadezer son of Rehob as a powerful ruler whose influence reached the Euphrates.
aram-zobah.r: According to the Bible, Hadadezer commanded chariots and allied Aramaean kingdoms, and rich towns of his land produced bronze. Little else is known, since no inscriptions from Zobah have been found.
aram-zobah.e: The Bible says David of the United Kingdom of Israel defeated Hadadezer and took his gold shields to Jerusalem, and that Rezon, a former officer, founded Aram-Damascus, which soon replaced Zobah as the leading Aramaean power.

anglo-egyptian-sudan.t: Sudan under a joint British and Egyptian condominium from 1899, in practice a British colony, until independence in 1956.
anglo-egyptian-sudan.o: After Kitchener's reconquest destroyed the Mahdist State, Britain and Egypt signed the Condominium Agreement in January 1899. Sovereignty was formally shared, but a British governor-general, appointed on British advice, held supreme authority.
anglo-egyptian-sudan.r: British officials governed through native administration, using tribal chiefs and sultans. The Gezira Scheme, opened in 1925, made irrigated cotton the main export. The south was administered separately under a Southern Policy that excluded northern influence and favoured Christian missions. After the assassination of governor-general Lee Stack in 1924, Egyptian troops were expelled.
anglo-egyptian-sudan.e: An Anglo-Egyptian agreement in 1953 provided for self-government and self-determination. Sudan became independent on 1 January 1956, but the separate treatment of the south contributed to a civil war that had already begun in 1955.
anglo-egyptian-sudan.re: Sunni Islam (north); traditional religions and Christianity (south)

ainu-chiefdoms.t: The self-governing communities of the Ainu, the indigenous people of Hokkaido, Sakhalin and the Kuril Islands, before Japanese annexation in 1869.
ainu-chiefdoms.o: Ainu culture took recognisable form around the 13th century in Hokkaido, growing out of the earlier Satsumon culture with influences from the Okhotsk culture. Ainu also lived in southern Sakhalin, the Kurils and northern Honshu. They called their land Ainu Mosir, the land of humans.
ainu-chiefdoms.r: There was no single state. Villages (kotan) led by elders formed regional groupings under powerful chiefs, who built hilltop forts called chashi. Ainu lived by hunting, fishing and trade, exchanging salmon, furs and hawks for Japanese rice, iron and lacquer and for Chinese silks via the Amur. Religion centred on kamuy spirits, honoured in rites such as the bear-sending ceremony.
ainu-chiefdoms.e: The Matsumae Domain imposed a trade monopoly; uprisings under Koshamain in 1457 and Shakushain in 1669 failed. Meiji Japan annexed Hokkaido in 1869 and pursued assimilation. Japan recognised the Ainu as an indigenous people in 2019.

ardalan.t: A Kurdish principality in western Iran that ruled for more than five centuries and made Sanandaj a centre of Kurdish literature.
ardalan.o: The Ardalan family traced its descent to a semi-legendary Baba Ardalan and emerged as rulers of the Kurdish lands around Sharazur and the Zagros by the 14th century. The principality lay on the frontier between the Ottoman Empire and the Safavid Empire, and the Ardalans shifted between them before settling mostly under Iranian overlordship.
ardalan.r: The Ardalan walis ruled a Sunni Kurdish population of farmers and tribes, sending troops and tribute to the shahs. Soleyman Khan Ardalan founded Sanandaj (Sinneh) in the 1630s as his capital. The court patronised poetry in Gorani, the literary Kurdish of the region, and in the 19th century Mastoureh Ardalan wrote a history of the dynasty, one of the first by a Kurdish woman. Amanullah Khan built palaces and gardens in Sanandaj.
ardalan.e: Qajar Iran steadily reduced Ardalan autonomy, and in 1867 Naser al-Din Shah replaced the last wali with a royal governor, ending the principality.

alash-autonomy.t: The Kazakh national government of the Alash party, which sought autonomy during the Russian Civil War and whose leaders were later killed in Stalin's purges.
alash-autonomy.o: The Alash party was founded by Kazakh intellectuals including Alikhan Bukeikhanov, Akhmet Baitursynov and Mirzhakip Dulatov. In December 1917 the Second All-Kazakh Congress in Orenburg proclaimed the Alash Autonomy and formed a government, the Alash Orda.
alash-autonomy.r: Alash Orda, led by Bukeikhanov, sought a Kazakh autonomy within a democratic Russian federation and governed from Semey (Semipalatinsk) with an eastern branch, while a western wing operated in Zhympity. It tried to build a militia and promoted Kazakh education and a reformed Arabic script. It allied with the Whites at times while negotiating with the Bolsheviks.
alash-autonomy.e: Disillusioned with the Whites, Alash leaders accepted Soviet power in 1919 and 1920, when the government was dissolved and the Kazakh lands became the Kirghiz, later Kazakh ASSR. Most of its leaders were executed in the purges of the 1930s; they were rehabilitated in the late Soviet period.

ah-kin-chel.t: A Maya province of north-central Yucatán, ruled by the priestly Chel lineage and including the old pilgrimage centre of Izamal.
ah-kin-chel.o: According to Bishop Diego de Landa, a priest of the Chel lineage at Mayapan foresaw its fall and, after its destruction around 1441, founded a new realm. The province took his title, Ah Kin (priest) Chel, and its capital was at Tecoh.
ah-kin-chel.r: Ah Kin Chel covered a large area of north-central Yucatán reaching the coast, with salt beds and fishing grounds. It included Izamal, a pilgrimage centre of the god Itzamna with massive ancient pyramids. Its ruler governed through the batabs of local towns, and the province maintained rivalries with Sotuta and Cupul.
ah-kin-chel.e: Ah Kin Chel submitted to the Spanish in the early 1540s and was absorbed into the Province of Yucatán. The Franciscans built a great convent on a pyramid at Izamal in the 1550s.

andros.t: Northernmost large island of the Cyclades, coloniser of the Chalcidice and remembered for defying Themistocles's demand for money in 480 BCE.
andros.o: Andros, just south-east of Euboea, was settled by Ionian Greeks in the early Iron Age. The fortified Geometric town of Zagora flourished in the 8th century BCE. Andros was long linked with Eretria, and c. 655 BCE Andrians founded colonies in the Chalcidice, including Acanthus, Stagira and Argilus.
andros.r: The island lived from farming, wine and seafaring. It sent ships to Xerxes in 480 BCE; when Themistocles demanded money, the Andrians replied that their gods were Poverty and Helplessness. Andros later paid tribute in the Delian League, and Athens planted a colony there c. 450 BCE. The marble Hermes of Andros shows its later prosperity.
andros.e: Under Hellenistic kings Andros changed hands often. Rome captured it in 199 BCE and handed it to Attalus I of the Kingdom of Pergamon, and it passed to direct Roman control after 133 BCE.

ajuran-sultanate.t: A Somali Muslim state that controlled the wells and rivers of southern Somalia and the Benadir coast, fighting off the Portuguese in the 16th century.
ajuran-sultanate.o: The Ajuran rose in the 13th century among Somali clans of the inter-riverine region between the Shabelle and Jubba rivers. Under the Garen dynasty, which claimed a holy Arab lineage, it extended its authority over pastoral clans of the interior and coastal cities such as Mogadishu, Merca and Barawa. Most of its history comes from oral tradition, supported by coins and ruins.
ajuran-sultanate.r: The Ajuran is often called a hydraulic state: it controlled wells and river water and taxed their use, as well as levying tribute in grain, cattle and goods. A governing hierarchy of governors and military commanders ran the provinces. It joined the coastal trade in ivory, cloth and grain, and in the 1580s cooperated with the Ottoman corsair Mir Ali Bey against the Portuguese.
ajuran-sultanate.e: Heavy taxation and the rule of a narrow elite provoked revolts in the late 17th century, and the sultanate broke up. The Hiraab Imamate took over the Mogadishu region and the Sultanate of the Geledi much of the Shabelle valley. Wells, forts and tombs attributed to the Ajuran survive across southern Somalia.

aenus.t: Aeolian city at the mouth of the Hebrus river in Thrace, a gateway for trade with the Thracian interior.
aenus.o: Aenus was founded by Aeolian settlers from Mytilene and Cyme on a hill at the mouth of the Hebrus, the modern Maritsa or Evros, on the Thracian coast. Homer mentions a Thracian named from Aenus, and the city flourished from the 6th century BCE.
aenus.r: Aenus traded salt fish and goods with the Thracian interior along the Hebrus, including the Odrysian Kingdom. It struck fine silver coins with the head of Hermes. Aenus paid tribute in the Delian League and fought on the Athenian side at Syracuse in 413 BCE.
aenus.e: In the Hellenistic period Aenus was held in turn by the Ptolemaic Empire and the Antigonid Kingdom of Macedonia. Rome declared it free in 167 BCE, and it came under Roman control by 146 BCE. It is today the Turkish town of Enez.

arcadian-league.t: Short-lived federation of the Arcadian cities created after Leuctra, which built Megalopolis and helped break Spartan power in the Peloponnese.
arcadian-league.o: Sparta's defeat at Leuctra in 371 BCE freed the Arcadians to act together. Led by Lycomedes of Mantinea and backed by Thebes, they formed a federal state in 370 BCE, and Mantinea was refounded. A new federal capital, Megalopolis, was built by uniting dozens of villages in south-western Arcadia.
arcadian-league.r: The league had an assembly known as the Ten Thousand, a federal council and magistrates, and a standing elite force, the eparitoi, paid from federal funds. It joined Thebes in invading Laconia and supported the refounding of Messene. Arcadian pride and a sense of common identity were expressed in federal coins and dedications.
arcadian-league.e: Quarrels with Elis led the Arcadians to seize Olympia, and disputes over using the sanctuary's treasure to pay the eparitoi split the league in 363 BCE, with Mantinea siding with Sparta and Tegea with Thebes. The Battle of Mantinea in 362 BCE left the federation broken, though Megalopolis endured.

ahmadili-dynasty.t: A line of Turkish atabegs that ruled Maragheh in Azerbaijan in the 12th century, rivals of the Eldiguzids for power in north-western Iran.
ahmadili-dynasty.o: Ahmadil ibn Ibrahim, a Kurdish emir of the Rawwadid family, held Maragheh under the Seljuk Empire until he was killed by the Nizari Ismailis in 1116. His Turkish mamluk Aq Sunqur Ahmadili succeeded him around 1122 and founded a dynasty named after his former master.
ahmadili-dynasty.r: The Ahmadilis governed Maragheh and its region as atabegs, nominally guardians of Seljuk princes, and took part in the struggles of the Seljuk Sultanate of Iraq. Aq Sunqur and his son Aq Sunqur II backed rival sultans against the Eldiguzids. Maragheh flourished as a regional city with fine brick tomb towers, such as the Gonbad-e Sorkh of 1147.
ahmadili-dynasty.e: The Mongols sacked Maragheh in 1221, and around 1225 the Khwarazmshah Jalal al-Din Mangburni took the city from the last representative of the dynasty, a woman ruler.

aequi.t: Mountain people east of Rome whose raids threatened Latium in the 5th century BCE, the enemies defeated by the legendary Cincinnatus.
aequi.o: The Aequi lived in the upper valleys of the Aniene, Turano and Salto rivers in the Apennines east of Latium. They were probably a Sabellic people, though their language is unknown. They appear in Roman history in the early 5th century BCE, pushing into the Latin plain through the pass of Mount Algidus.
aequi.r: Known only from Roman sources, the Aequi lived in small fortified hill settlements and raided the farmland of Latium, often in alliance with the Volsci. Their most famous episode is Cincinnatus's rescue of a trapped Roman army at Mount Algidus in 458 BCE.
aequi.e: Rome gradually drove them back. In 304 BCE, Livy says, Rome captured 31 of their towns in 50 days and almost wiped out the people. Roman colonies were planted at Alba Fucens in 303 BCE and Carseoli in 298 BCE, and surviving Aequian communities became Roman.

alupa-dynasty.t: The long-lived rulers of Tulu Nadu on the Karnataka coast, who survived for more than a thousand years as vassals of greater powers.
alupa-dynasty.o: The Alupas ruled the coastal strip of Karnataka between the Western Ghats and the Arabian Sea. Ptolemy may refer to their land as Olokhoira in the 2nd century, and they appear in inscriptions from the 7th century as feudatories of the Chalukyas of Badami. Earlier they probably served the Kadamba dynasty.
alupa-dynasty.r: Their capitals moved from Udyavara to Mangalore and later Barkur. Alupa kings issued distinctive gold and copper coins and ruled through local chiefs, profiting from the trade of the Kanara ports with Arabia and the Persian Gulf. They acknowledged the supremacy in turn of the Chalukyas, the Rashtrakuta dynasty and the Hoysala Empire, and patronised Shaiva and Jain temples. Their inscriptions are among the earliest in Kannada.
alupa-dynasty.e: From the 14th century the Alupas came under the Vijayanagara Empire, and their line ends in the records around 1444, when Tulu Nadu was absorbed into Vijayanagara administration. The region kept its distinct Tulu language and culture.

apalachee-chiefdom.t: A maize-farming chiefdom of the Florida Panhandle that met de Soto, became the heart of Spain's mission system and was destroyed by English-led raids in 1704.
apalachee-chiefdom.o: The Apalachee emerged from the Fort Walton culture, the Mississippian tradition of the region between the Aucilla and Ochlockonee rivers around modern Tallahassee, from around 1100. The Lake Jackson mounds were an early centre. When Pánfilo de Narváez arrived in 1528 and Hernando de Soto wintered at their capital, Anhaica, in 1539 to 1540, the Apalachee were populous and warlike.
apalachee-chiefdom.r: Chiefs ruled from towns with mounds and plazas, and the fertile red clay hills produced large maize surpluses. The Apalachee were famous for a ball game with ritual meaning. Franciscan missions began in 1633, and many Apalachee became Catholic, sending maize and labour to St Augustine. Mission San Luis de Talimali, founded in 1656, became the capital of western Spanish Florida, housing Apalachee leaders alongside Spanish soldiers.
apalachee-chiefdom.e: In 1704 Carolina's former governor James Moore and Muscogee allies destroyed most missions, killing or enslaving thousands. Survivors scattered to Pensacola, to Mobile in French Louisiana, or joined the Muscogee. Descendants survive in Louisiana as the Talimali Band of Apalachee.

athmallik-state.t: A princely state on the Mahanadi in central Odisha, ruled from Kaintragarh until 1948.
athmallik-state.o: Tradition dates the ruling family to around 1500, but little is reliably known of its founding. The name refers to the eight mallis, or divisions, of its territory.
athmallik-state.r: Athmallik was a forested, thinly populated state on the south bank of the Mahanadi. It was linked with the Sambalpur group of chiefships under the Marathas and passed under British supervision in the 19th century, joining the Orissa Tributary States in 1905. Its history is poorly recorded.
athmallik-state.e: Athmallik merged into Orissa on 1 January 1948 and is now in Angul district.

aghlabid-emirate.t: The Aghlabid emirs of Ifriqiya, who ruled Tunisia for the Abbasids, built Kairouan's Great Mosque and conquered Sicily.
aghlabid-emirate.o: In 800 the Abbasid caliph Harun al-Rashid granted Ibrahim ibn al-Aghlab, an Arab army commander, the governorship of Ifriqiya as a hereditary office in return for annual tribute. The Aghlabids ruled from Kairouan and their palace city al-Abbasiyya, and later Raqqada, as autonomous emirs of the Abbasid Caliphate.
aghlabid-emirate.r: Relying on an Arab military elite and slave soldiers, they faced frequent army revolts. Ziyadat Allah I launched the conquest of Byzantine Sicily in 827, and Aghlabid fleets raided Italy and took Malta in 870. They rebuilt the Great Mosque of Kairouan, built the ribat of Sousse and great water cisterns, and Kairouan became a centre of Maliki law under the jurist Sahnun.
aghlabid-emirate.e: In the 890s the Kutama Berbers, mobilised by the Ismaili missionary Abu Abdallah al-Shi'i, rose against them. In 909 the last emir, Ziyadat Allah III, fled to the east, and the Fatimid Caliphate was proclaimed in Ifriqiya.

akyem-abuakwa.t: Akan kingdom of the eastern Gold Coast forest, rich in gold and later a stronghold of the cocoa economy, ruled by the Okyenhene from Kyebi.
akyem-abuakwa.o: The Akyem peoples moved into the forest of the Birim valley by the 16th century, and Akyem Abuakwa became the largest of their states. It lay across the routes from the coast to the interior, near rich gold deposits.
akyem-abuakwa.r: The Okyenhene ruled with divisional chiefs, queen mothers and the councils typical of Akan states. Akyem Abuakwa mined gold and traded it to the coast. In 1730, under Ofori Panin, it joined with Akyem Kotoku and the Ga to overthrow Akwamu. It then fought the Ashanti Empire for decades, sometimes as its tributary and sometimes as a rebel.
akyem-abuakwa.e: Akyem Abuakwa allied with the British against Ashanti and came under British rule with the Gold Coast Colony in 1874. In the 20th century it became a heartland of cocoa farming, and the Okyenhene still reigns at Kyebi.

ara-gaya.t: A major Gaya kingdom at Haman, known for its flame-pattern stoneware and as host of diplomatic conferences between Baekje, Silla and Japan.
ara-gaya.o: Ara Gaya, the Anra of Japanese sources, developed from Anya-guk, a Byeonhan statelet in the Haman basin southwest of the Nakdong. According to Korean chronicles it was attacked in the early 3rd century by the eight port states of the coast and saved by Silla.
ara-gaya.r: After Geumgwan Gaya declined around 400, Ara Gaya became, with Daegaya, one of the two leading Gaya states. Hilltop tombs at Malisan hold armour, horse gear and distinctive stoneware with flame-shaped openings. In the 6th century it convened talks with envoys of Baekje, Silla and Yamato as the Gaya states tried to survive between their neighbours.
ara-gaya.e: Caught between Baekje and Silla, Ara Gaya was taken by Silla around 560, shortly before the fall of Daegaya, and became a Silla county.

alipura-state.t: A small Parihar Rajput state of the Bundelkhand Agency in central India.
alipura-state.o: Alipura became a separate chiefship in the mid-18th century under a Parihar Rajput family, during the break-up of Bundela power in Bundelkhand. It was confirmed by a British sanad in the early 19th century.
alipura-state.r: Its ruler governed a small rural territory as a non-salute state. Little else is recorded about its internal history.
alipura-state.e: After independence Alipura was merged with the other Bundelkhand states into Vindhya Pradesh, and its lands were absorbed into the Indian administration by 1950; the town is in Chhatarpur district of Madhya Pradesh.

albanian-kingdom-1939-1943.t: Albania under Italian occupation, joined to Italy in a personal union under King Victor Emmanuel III and used as a base for the invasion of Greece.
albanian-kingdom-1939-1943.o: Italy invaded Albania on 7 April 1939, forcing King Zog of the Albanian Kingdom into exile. A constituent assembly summoned in Tirana offered the crown to Victor Emmanuel III, creating a personal union with Italy. Shefqet Vërlaci, a large landowner and rival of Zog, became prime minister under an Italian lieutenant-general, Francesco Jacomoni.
albanian-kingdom-1939-1943.r: Real power lay with Italian officials: Albania's army and foreign service were merged into Italy's and an Albanian Fascist Party was created. Italy launched its invasion of Greece from Albanian soil in October 1940, and after the conquest of Yugoslavia in 1941 Kosovo and western Macedonia were added, forming a Greater Albania. Resistance grew, including Enver Hoxha's Communist Party, founded in 1941.
albanian-kingdom-1939-1943.e: When Italy capitulated in September 1943, German troops occupied Albania and created the Albanian Kingdom (1943-1944), a nominally independent state under German control. Victor Emmanuel III formally renounced the Albanian crown in 1943, and the union with Italy was never restored.
albanian-kingdom-1939-1943.re: Sunni Islam, Orthodox and Catholic Christianity

arevaci.t: The strongest of the Celtiberian peoples, defenders of Numantia, whose siege by Scipio Aemilianus in 134 to 133 BCE became a byword for resistance.
arevaci.o: The Arevaci occupied the upper Douro basin in modern Soria and Segovia from about the 4th century BCE. Strabo called them the most powerful of the Celtiberians, and their towns included Numantia, Termes and Uxama.
arevaci.r: They lived in large fortified towns with grid-like streets, governed by councils and elected war leaders. Numantia's pottery shows painted horses and warriors. Herding, cereal growing and iron working sustained them, and their warriors were renowned in Roman sources for courage and skill with the sword.
arevaci.e: From 153 BCE they led resistance to Rome, defeating several consuls. In 134 BCE Scipio Aemilianus surrounded Numantia with walls and starved it; Retogenes broke out to seek aid, but the town fell in 133 BCE. The Arevaci later backed Sertorius before becoming part of Hispania Citerior.

alirajpur-state.t: A Rathore Rajput state in the Bhil hills of western Madhya Pradesh, birthplace of the revolutionary Chandra Shekhar Azad.
alirajpur-state.o: The ruling Rathore family established itself in the hills south of the Malwa plateau; tradition dates the state to 1437. Its early history is poorly recorded.
alirajpur-state.r: Alirajpur was a hilly, forested state whose people were mostly Bhils and Bhilalas, known for the Bhagoria spring festival. It paid tribute to the Marathas and later came under the Bhopawar Agency of British central India. Chandra Shekhar Azad was born in the state's village of Bhabhra in 1906.
alirajpur-state.e: Alirajpur merged into Madhya Bharat in 1948, which became part of Madhya Pradesh in 1956. It is now a district of Madhya Pradesh.

arakkal-kingdom.t: The only Muslim royal house of Kerala, the Ali Rajas of Cannanore, who ruled a coastal principality and the Lakshadweep islands.
arakkal-kingdom.o: The Arakkal family were Mappila Muslim ministers and admirals of the Kolathiri rulers of Kolathunadu, based at Cannanore. By the 16th century, as the Portuguese disrupted the coast, they became an autonomous power, holding the title Ali Raja, lord of the sea, and ruling the town and the Lakshadweep islands.
arakkal-kingdom.r: The Arakkal rulers followed matrilineal succession, so that the eldest member of the family, male or female, reigned; several women ruled with the title Arakkal Beevi. Their wealth came from trade in pepper, coir and cowries and from the islands. They opposed the Portuguese and later allied with Hyder Ali of the Kingdom of Mysore.
arakkal-kingdom.e: The British East India Company captured Cannanore in 1790 and later took over the Lakshadweep islands in return for a pension; the family's political authority ended by 1819. The Arakkal family survives in Kannur and maintains a museum in its old palace.

appenzell-innerrhoden.t: The Catholic half of Appenzell, created by the canton's division in 1597, which still governs itself by an open-air assembly.
appenzell-innerrhoden.o: In 1597 the Canton of Appenzell, divided by the Reformation, was split in two with the mediation of the other Swiss cantons. The Catholic inner districts around the village of Appenzell formed Innerrhoden, keeping the old seat and archives.
appenzell-innerrhoden.r: Innerrhoden governed itself through its Landsgemeinde, meeting in the square at Appenzell, which elected the Landammann and passed laws. It shared a single vote in the federal Diet with Ausserrhoden. The economy rested on cattle and dairy farming and later on embroidery done at home. Capuchin friars strengthened the Counter-Reformation.
appenzell-innerrhoden.e: The French invasion of 1798 merged Appenzell into the canton of Säntis of the Helvetic Republic. Restored in 1803, Innerrhoden still holds its Landsgemeinde; it was the last canton to give women the vote, in 1990, after a federal court ruling.

aland.t: Demilitarised, Swedish-speaking island autonomy within Finland, created by a League of Nations decision in 1921 and still self-governing today.
aland.o: The Åland Islands, between Sweden and Finland, passed to Russia with Finland in 1809 and were demilitarised after the Crimean War in 1856. When Finland became independent, most Ålanders, who speak Swedish, wanted to join Sweden. The League of Nations ruled in 1921 that the islands belonged to Finland, but with guaranteed autonomy and protection of the Swedish language.
aland.r: Åland governs itself through its own parliament, the Lagting, first convened in 1922 under Julius Sundblom, and a government in Mariehamn, with powers over education, culture, policing and local economy. Swedish is the only official language, and the right of domicile restricts land ownership to residents. The islands remain demilitarised and neutral, and their economy rests on shipping, ferries and tourism.
aland.e: Autonomy has been widened by later acts, and Åland gained its own flag in 1954 and its own stamps in 1984. When Finland joined the EU in 1995, Åland kept a special status outside the EU tax area. It remains an autonomous region of the Republic of Finland.

ahhiyawa.t: A Late Bronze Age power named in some thirty Hittite texts, widely identified with the Mycenaean Greeks, the Achaeans of Homer.
ahhiyawa.o: The name Ahhiyawa, close to Homer's Achaeans, appears in Hittite records from c. 1400 BCE, when a 'man of Ahhiya' named Attarissiya raided western Anatolia and Alashiya. Most scholars now accept that it denotes a Mycenaean Greek kingdom, or a coalition of them, though its centre is debated, with Mycenae, Thebes and Rhodes all proposed.
ahhiyawa.r: In the 13th century BCE a Hittite king addressed the king of Ahhiyawa as a 'Great King' and 'brother', ranking him with Egypt, Babylon and Assyria. Ahhiyawa held Millawanda on the Anatolian coast and backed rebels such as Piyamaradu. Hittite texts mention ships from Ahhiyawa and a dispute over Wilusa, often linked with Troy.
ahhiyawa.e: In a treaty of Tudhaliya IV, c. 1230 BCE, the king of Ahhiyawa was struck from the list of great kings, suggesting its power had waned. References cease soon after, as the Mycenaean palaces collapsed c. 1200 BCE.

ayyubid-emirate-of-hama.t: The longest-surviving Ayyubid principality, which lasted under Mamluk overlordship and was ruled by the historian and geographer Abu al-Fida.
ayyubid-emirate-of-hama.o: In 1178 Saladin granted Hama on the Orontes to his nephew Taqi al-Din Umar, whose descendants kept it as a hereditary principality within the Ayyubid family confederation.
ayyubid-emirate-of-hama.r: Hama's rulers usually sided with the sultans in Egypt against their cousins in Damascus and Aleppo. Al-Mansur Muhammad II joined the Mamluks against the Mongols in 1260 and was allowed to keep his throne as a vassal. The principality was known for its learned princes: Abu al-Fida, appointed ruler in 1310 by the Mamluk sultan al-Nasir Muhammad, wrote a universal history and the geographical work Taqwim al-Buldan. The great waterwheels of the Orontes irrigated its gardens.
ayyubid-emirate-of-hama.e: After Abu al-Fida's death in 1331, his son al-Afdal Muhammad was deposed in 1341, and Hama became an ordinary Mamluk province.

arjunayanas.t: A small republic of north-eastern Rajasthan, known from its coins, which claimed descent from the epic hero Arjuna.
arjunayanas.o: The Arjunayanas are known mainly from coins and from one inscription. They took their name from Arjuna, the Pandava hero of the Mahabharata, and appear to have emerged as an independent gana in the Bharatpur and Alwar region after the fall of the Maurya Empire.
arjunayanas.r: Their copper coins, dated to around the 1st century BCE, bear the legend Arjunayananam jayah, victory of the Arjunayanas, which shows they were governed as a republic rather than by a king. Nothing more is known of their society.
arjunayanas.e: In the 4th century the Arjunayanas were among the peoples that submitted to Samudragupta of the Gupta Empire, according to his Allahabad pillar inscription, after which they disappear from the record.

antigua-and-barbuda.t: Two-island Leeward state independent since 1981, long dominated by the Bird family and now reliant on tourism.
antigua-and-barbuda.o: The Colony of Antigua, with Barbuda and Redonda, became independent on 1 November 1981. Vere Bird, the trade unionist who had led the Antigua Labour Party since the 1940s, became the first prime minister, with the British monarch as head of state. Barbudans had sought separate status and remained uneasy partners.
antigua-and-barbuda.r: The Antigua Labour Party under Vere Bird and then his son Lester Bird governed until 2004, amid scandals including the shipment of Israeli arms through Antigua to the Medellín cartel in 1989 to 1990. Tourism, with beaches and the restored Nelson's Dockyard, replaced sugar, and the country also developed offshore finance and online gambling. The collapse of Allen Stanford's banking empire in 2009 was a severe blow.
antigua-and-barbuda.e: Baldwin Spencer's United Progressive Party ruled from 2004 to 2014, and Gaston Browne has led governments since 2014. Hurricane Irma forced the evacuation of Barbuda in 2017, and disputes over communal land on Barbuda have continued.

archbishopric-of-magdeburg.t: Otto the Great's favoured archbishopric on the Elbe, head of the church in the Slavic east, which became a Protestant territory and then part of Brandenburg-Prussia.
archbishopric-of-magdeburg.o: Otto I founded a monastery at Magdeburg in 937 and, after years of negotiation with the Pope and the Archbishop of Mainz, raised it to an archbishopric in 968, with suffragans at Merseburg, Meissen, Zeitz (later Naumburg), Brandenburg and Havelberg. Otto and his first wife, Edith of England, are buried in the cathedral.
archbishopric-of-magdeburg.r: The archbishops ruled a territory along the middle Elbe and Saale. Archbishop Wichmann granted Magdeburg its town law around 1188, a model copied across central and eastern Europe. The Gothic cathedral, begun in 1209, was the first in Germany. Albert of Brandenburg's sale of indulgences as archbishop prompted Luther's theses in 1517.
archbishopric-of-magdeburg.e: Magdeburg became Lutheran, ruled by Protestant administrators, and the city was sacked by imperial troops in 1631. The Peace of Westphalia assigned the archbishopric to Brandenburg on the death of its administrator, which happened in 1680, when it became the Duchy of Magdeburg within Brandenburg-Prussia.

abdera-800.t: A Phoenician trading port on the coast of Almería, at modern Adra, that later minted coins under Carthaginian and Roman rule.
abdera-800.o: Phoenician settlers founded Abdera in the 8th century BCE on the hill of Montecristo at modern Adra, at the mouth of the river Adra. It was one of a chain of Phoenician harbours along the southern coast of Iberia, with Sexi and Malaka, linking Gadir with the eastern Mediterranean.
abdera-800.r: Little is known of its government. Like its neighbours, Abdera lived from trade with the Iberian hinterland, fishing and the salting of fish. In the Punic period it fell under the influence of Carthage, and its later coins, inscribed in Punic letters, showed a temple facade with tuna fish.
abdera-800.e: After the Roman victory over Carthage in Hispania in 206 BCE Abdera came under Rome, keeping its coinage into the early empire. It continued as a small Roman town, and Strabo listed it among the Phoenician foundations of the coast.

argos.t: Ancient city of the Argolid, Sparta's enduring rival in the Peloponnese, famed for the sanctuary of Hera and the sculptor Polykleitos.
argos.o: Argos lies in the Argive plain below the Larisa and Aspis hills and was inhabited from the Bronze Age. In the early Iron Age Dorian settlers made it the leading city of the Argolid. In the 7th century BCE King Pheidon, credited with standard measures, made it the strongest power in the Peloponnese, and Argos beat Sparta at Hysiai c. 669 BCE.
argos.r: Argos controlled the great Heraion between it and Mycenae and was a centre of bronze sculpture, home of Hageladas and Polykleitos. Its power was broken when Cleomenes I of Sparta destroyed its army at Sepeia c. 494 BCE. Argos stayed neutral in 480 BCE, then destroyed Mycenae and Tiryns and adopted democracy.
argos.e: Allied with Athens, Argos was defeated at Mantinea in 418 BCE. Pyrrhus of the Kingdom of Epirus died fighting in its streets in 272 BCE. Argos joined the Achaean League in 229 BCE and passed under Rome in 146 BCE.

azerbaijan-democratic-republic.t: The first parliamentary republic in the Muslim world, founded in 1918, which granted women the vote before it fell to the Red Army in 1920.
azerbaijan-democratic-republic.o: As the Transcaucasian Democratic Federative Republic dissolved, the Azerbaijani National Council declared independence in Tiflis on 28 May 1918. Its government moved to Ganja and, with the help of the Ottoman Army of Islam, took Baku from the Centrocaspian Dictatorship in September 1918, making it the capital.
azerbaijan-democratic-republic.r: The republic was led by the Musavat party under Mammad Amin Rasulzade and prime ministers such as Fatali Khan Khoyski, with a multi-party parliament that included minority representatives. It granted women the vote in 1919, founded Baku State University and adopted the blue, red and green flag. Baku's oil was its economic base, but it faced conflicts with Armenia over Karabakh and Zangezur.
azerbaijan-democratic-republic.e: In April 1920 the Red Army invaded, and the government ceded power to the Bolsheviks, creating the Azerbaijan SSR. The independent Republic of Azerbaijan in 1991 adopted its flag and declared itself its successor.

aduatuci.t: Belgic people said to descend from Cimbri and Teutones, whose entire population was sold into slavery by Caesar in 57 BCE.
aduatuci.o: Caesar says the Aduatuci descended from six thousand Cimbri and Teutones left to guard the baggage of the great migration before 102 BCE, who settled on the middle Meuse. Their stronghold is usually placed near Namur or Thuin in Belgium.
aduatuci.r: They imposed tribute on their neighbours, including the Eburones, and fortified a hilltop oppidum.
aduatuci.e: In 57 BCE they surrendered to Caesar but attacked his camp at night with hidden weapons. Caesar stormed the oppidum and sold the inhabitants, fifty-three thousand by his count, into slavery. Survivors joined Ambiorix in 54 BCE, after which the name disappears.

ahmadnagar-sultanate.t: The Nizam Shahi sultanate of the northern Deccan, remembered for Chand Bibi's defence of Ahmadnagar and Malik Ambar's resistance to the Mughals.
ahmadnagar-sultanate.o: Malik Ahmad Nizam Shah, son of a Bahmani minister, defeated a Bahmani army in 1490 and declared independence. In 1494 he founded the city of Ahmadnagar as his capital, establishing the Nizam Shahi dynasty in the northern Deccan.
ahmadnagar-sultanate.r: The Nizam Shahs annexed the Berar Sultanate in 1574 and took part in the victory over the Vijayanagara Empire at Talikota. Chand Bibi, acting as regent, defended Ahmadnagar against Mughal attack in 1595. After the capital fell, the Ethiopian-born minister Malik Ambar kept the state alive from Khadki (later Aurangabad), pioneering guerrilla warfare and a land revenue survey later adopted by the Mughals.
ahmadnagar-sultanate.e: Ahmadnagar fell to the Mughal Empire in 1600, but resistance continued under Malik Ambar and his son. Shahaji Bhonsle, a Maratha general, propped up a puppet Nizam Shah until Shah Jahan forced his surrender in 1636 and annexed the remaining territory.

ambiani.t: Belgic people of the Somme valley whose town Samarobriva, modern Amiens, hosted Caesar's council of Gaul in 54 BCE.
ambiani.o: The Ambiani held the lower and middle Somme in Picardy. Caesar records that they promised ten thousand warriors to the Belgic league of 57 BCE and surrendered after the league broke up.
ambiani.r: Their oppidum of Samarobriva, the bridge on the Samara or Somme, controlled a key crossing. They struck abundant gold coins, some of the earliest in northern Gaul.
ambiani.e: Caesar held an assembly of the Gallic peoples at Samarobriva in 54 BCE and wintered there. The Ambiani sent men to relieve Alesia in 52 BCE and fought again in 51 BCE. Under Rome Samarobriva became a major city, later Ambianum, the origin of Amiens.

aedui.t: Leading people of central Gaul and Rome's oldest Gallic ally, whose quarrels with their rivals gave Caesar his pretext to invade Gaul.
aedui.o: The Aedui held the land between the Loire and the Saône, in modern Burgundy, with their great oppidum at Bibracte on Mont Beuvray. By the 2nd century BCE they were hailed by the Roman Senate as brothers and kinsmen of the Roman people, and they contested leadership of Gaul with the Arverni and the Sequani.
aedui.r: Government was oligarchic: a council of nobles and an annual chief magistrate, the vergobret, who could not leave the territory during office. Bibracte was a large town of craftsmen, enamellers and traders importing Italian wine. The druid Diviciacus spoke for Rome in the Senate, while his brother Dumnorix led the anti-Roman party.
aedui.e: Pressed by the Sequani and Ariovistus, the Aedui called on Caesar in 58 BCE, but in 52 BCE they joined Vercingetorix, who was chosen supreme leader at Bibracte. Pardoned after Alesia, they moved to the new city of Augustodunum (Autun), and in 48 CE Claudius admitted Aeduan nobles to the Roman Senate.

atrebates.t: Belgic people of Artois whose king Commius served Caesar, then turned against him and founded a dynasty in Britain.
atrebates.o: The Atrebates lived in the modern Artois around Nemetocenna (Arras). They joined the Belgic league in 57 BCE, promising fifteen thousand men, and fought beside the Nervii at the Sabis.
atrebates.r: After their defeat Caesar made Commius their king and used him as an envoy to the Britons in 55 BCE, extending his authority over the Morini. Their coins and their links across the Channel show close ties with Britain, where a people of the same name lived.
atrebates.e: Commius joined the great revolt of 52 BCE, helped lead the relief army at Alesia and later fled to Britain, where coins name his successors among the British Atrebates. Under Rome Nemetocenna became a civitas capital, the origin of Arras, and the name survives in Artois.

acragas.t: Greek city of south-west Sicily, famed for its temples and wealth, home of the philosopher Empedocles, which Pindar called the most beautiful city of mortals.
acragas.o: Colonists from Gela, with Rhodians, founded Acragas around 580 BCE on a ridge above the confluence of the Akragas and Hypsas rivers, near Sicily's south coast. Within a few decades it was one of the largest Greek cities.
acragas.r: The tyrant Phalaris, notorious for roasting enemies in a bronze bull, ruled around 570–554 BCE. Under Theron, who with Gelon defeated Carthage at Himera in 480 BCE, Acragas grew rich on grain, olives and trade with Carthage. Prisoners built temples along the southern ridge, today's Valley of the Temples, including the Temple of Concord and the colossal Olympieion. The philosopher Empedocles helped restore democracy there.
acragas.e: Carthage sacked Acragas in 406 BCE. Revived by Timoleon, it was taken by Rome in 262 BCE, retaken by Carthage, and finally captured by Rome in 210 BCE, becoming Agrigentum. The modern city, Agrigento, overlooks the temples, a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

alawi-sheikhdom.t: One of the smallest states of the Aden Protectorate, a tribal sheikhdom near the Yemeni frontier.
alawi-sheikhdom.o: The Alawi sheikhdom was a small tribal territory in the hills north of Aden, near Dhala, with its seat at Al Qasha. Like its neighbours, it gained independence in the 18th century as the Qasimid State withdrew from the south. Its early history is barely recorded.
alawi-sheikhdom.r: The sheikhs ruled a few thousand people by tribal custom. The territory entered British protection through treaties in the late 19th century and was part of the Western Aden Protectorate. In 1965 it joined the Federation of South Arabia, the British-sponsored union of protectorate states.
alawi-sheikhdom.e: After the National Liberation Front took power in 1967, the sheikhdom was abolished and absorbed into South Yemen.

amarnagar-state.t: A minor chiefship of southern Kathiawar, one of the small estates under British supervision.
amarnagar-state.o: Amarnagar, earlier known as Thana Amarnagar, was a small estate in Kathiawar held by a local chiefly family from around 1700. Its founding is poorly documented.
amarnagar-state.r: The ruler held a few villages and, after 1807, came under British supervision in the Kathiawar Agency. Standard references record little else of its history.
amarnagar-state.e: Amarnagar merged into the United State of Saurashtra in 1948 and became part of Gujarat in 1960.

adamawa-emirate.t: The largest emirate of the Sokoto Caliphate, stretching from the Benue into what is now Cameroon, and split by Britain and Germany in 1901.
adamawa-emirate.o: Modibbo Adama, a Fulani scholar, received a flag from Usman dan Fodio in 1809 to spread the jihad in Fombina, the southern lands. His followers conquered or absorbed many local chiefdoms on the upper Benue and the Cameroon highlands, and in 1841 Adama founded Yola as the capital.
adamawa-emirate.r: The emirate was a loose federation of dozens of sub-emirates, or lamidates, such as Ngaoundere, Garoua and Banyo, each ruled by a Fulani lamido who paid tribute to Yola, which in turn paid tribute to Sokoto. Slave raiding against non-Muslim peoples supplied tribute and labour, and the region was among the largest slave-holding societies in Africa. Lawal, Adama's son, ruled from 1847 to 1872.
adamawa-emirate.e: In 1901 British forces took Yola and Emir Zubeiru fled; the Anglo-German border gave most of the emirate to Kamerun. The British part became Adamawa Province in Northern Nigeria, and the Lamido of Adamawa still reigns at Yola.

antemoro-kingdom.t: A south-east Malagasy kingdom of Islamic-influenced clans whose scribes kept the sorabe, Malagasy texts written in Arabic script.
antemoro-kingdom.o: The Antemoro formed around the Matitana river near Vohipeno in south-east Madagascar, where clans claiming descent from Muslim immigrants established a ruling aristocracy around 1500. Their traditions trace the founders to Mecca, though the migrants probably came via the Swahili coast or the Comoros.
antemoro-kingdom.r: Power lay with the Anteony noble clans, while scribal and priestly clans, the Anakara, guarded the sorabe manuscripts on astrology, medicine, history and divination. Antemoro diviners (ombiasy) became sought after as advisers at other Malagasy courts, including the Merina Kingdom. Society was rigidly stratified, and the kingdom produced distinctive paper made from bark.
antemoro-kingdom.e: Internal revolts in the 17th century weakened the noble clans, and in the 19th century the region fell under the Merina Kingdom. French colonial rule followed in 1895–96. The Antemoro remain one of Madagascar's ethnic groups, still known for their sorabe and Antaimoro paper.
antemoro-kingdom.re: Traditional Malagasy religion with Islamic elements

audumbara.t: A people of the Punjab hills whose coins carry some of the earliest images of a Hindu temple.
audumbara.o: The Audumbaras are mentioned by the grammarian Panini and later texts as a people of the north-west. Coins show that by the 2nd and 1st centuries BCE they formed a state in the region between the Ravi and the Beas, around modern Pathankot and the Kangra valley.
audumbara.r: Little is known beyond their coinage. Their coins, with legends in Brahmi and Kharoshthi, name rulers such as Dharaghosha, Shivadasa and Rudradasa, and some show a pillared shrine beside a trident, one of the earliest depictions of a temple in India. The emphasis on Shiva and the trident points to a strong Shaiva cult, and the name comes from the udumbara fig tree.
audumbara.e: The Audumbaras appear to have lost their independence to the Indo-Scythians or the Kushan Empire in the 1st century, after which their coinage ends.

abuja-emirate.t: The refuge state of the Hausa rulers of Zazzau, who kept their independence from the Sokoto Caliphate and whose town gave its name to Nigeria's capital.
abuja-emirate.o: When Fulani jihadists took Zaria in 1808, the Hausa ruler of the Kingdom of Zazzau, Muhammadu Makau, fled south with his followers to Zuba. After his death his brother Abu Ja, also called Jatau, founded a new walled town around 1828, which took his name, Abuja, and became the capital of the exiled dynasty.
abuja-emirate.r: Abuja kept the titles and court ceremonial of old Zazzau and remained outside the Sokoto Caliphate, repelling attacks from the Zaria Emirate and other Fulani forces. Its rulers were Muslims, but they governed a mixed population of Hausa and Gbagyi farmers. The town became known for crafts such as weaving, pottery and metalwork, and for trade along the routes to the Niger.
abuja-emirate.e: British forces brought Abuja under the Protectorate of Northern Nigeria in 1902, and its emir kept his title. In 1976, when the new federal capital was given the name Abuja, the old town was renamed Suleja.

atabegs-of-yazd.t: A line of local rulers who governed the desert city of Yazd for nearly two centuries under the Seljuks, Khwarazmians and Mongols.
atabegs-of-yazd.o: Yazd had been held by the last members of the Kakuyid dynasty as vassals of the Seljuk Empire. Around 1141 the Seljuk sultan appointed Rukn al-Din Sam, son of a Turkish officer named Langar, as atabeg to the Kakuyid heiresses, and his family took over the city, founding the dynasty sometimes called the Langarids.
atabegs-of-yazd.r: The atabegs ruled a small oasis state around Yazd and Abarquh, living from irrigated farming by qanats, silk weaving and caravan trade across the central desert. They built mosques, madrasas and gardens in Yazd and paid tribute to whoever dominated Iran, including the Khwarazmian Empire and, from the 1250s, the Ilkhanate.
atabegs-of-yazd.e: In 1319 Mubariz al-Din Muhammad, founder of the Muzaffarid dynasty, defeated the last atabeg, Haji Shah, and took Yazd, which became the base of the Muzaffarids.

american-samoa.t: The eastern Samoan islands ceded to the United States from 1900, an unincorporated territory where Samoan custom and communal land endure.
american-samoa.o: The Tripartite Convention of 1899 ended the Kingdom of Samoa and gave the islands east of longitude 171 west to the United States, which prized the harbour of Pago Pago as a coaling station. Chiefs of Tutuila and Aunuʻu signed a deed of cession in 1900, and the rulers of the Kingdom of Manuʻa ceded their islands in 1904.
american-samoa.r: The US Navy governed the territory until 1951 through naval commandants, leaving village affairs and land to the matai, the chiefs of extended families. A local Mau movement in the 1920s protested naval rule. Authority passed to the Department of the Interior in 1951, and a constitution was adopted in 1967. Tuna canning became the main industry.
american-samoa.e: American Samoans elected their first governor, Peter Tali Coleman, in 1977. The territory remains unincorporated and unorganised; its people are US nationals rather than citizens, an arrangement many defend as protecting communal land and the faʻa Samoa way of life.
american-samoa.re: Protestantism, Roman Catholicism, Latter-day Saint movement

abhira-dynasty.t: A Deccan dynasty that took over the Nashik region from the Satavahanas and founded the era later used by the Kalachuris.
abhira-dynasty.o: The Abhiras were a pastoral people of western India, first serving as generals under the Western Satraps. As the Satavahana dynasty weakened in the early 3rd century, an Abhira chief, Ishvarasena, established a kingdom around Nashik in Maharashtra. An era beginning in 248 or 249, perhaps founded by him, was later known as the Kalachuri-Chedi era.
abhira-dynasty.r: The dynasty is known mainly from a Prakrit inscription of Ishvarasena at the Buddhist caves of Nashik, recording an endowment by a laywoman, and from coins. The Puranas say ten Abhira kings ruled. They seem to have controlled northern Maharashtra and parts of Gujarat and Konkan.
abhira-dynasty.e: The Abhira kingdom declined in the 4th century; the Allahabad pillar inscription lists the Abhiras among peoples who submitted to Samudragupta of the Gupta Empire. Their lands passed to the Traikutakas and later to the Kalachuris of Mahishmati.

ashanti-colony.t: The British colony created from the conquered Ashanti Empire after the War of the Golden Stool, which joined independent Ghana in 1957.
ashanti-colony.o: British forces occupied Kumasi in 1896 and exiled the Asantehene Prempeh I, eventually to the Seychelles. In 1900 the governor's demand for the Golden Stool, the sacred symbol of the Asante nation, provoked a rising led by Yaa Asantewaa, queen mother of Ejisu. After its suppression Britain annexed Ashanti as a crown colony on 1 January 1902.
ashanti-colony.r: A chief commissioner at Kumasi governed through Asante chiefs. The colony became the heart of Gold Coast cocoa production, and Kumasi grew into a major commercial centre linked by rail to the coast. Prempeh I was allowed to return in 1924, and in 1935 the British restored the Asante Confederacy under his successor Prempeh II.
ashanti-colony.e: In the 1950s the National Liberation Movement, based in Ashanti, demanded a federal constitution, but on 6 March 1957 Ashanti became part of a unitary Ghana. The Asantehene remains the most influential traditional ruler in the country.

agathyrsi.t: Gold-rich people of Transylvania described by Herodotus, known for tattoos, luxury and refusing to join the Scythians against Persia.
agathyrsi.o: Herodotus places the Agathyrsi along the Maris (Mureș) in Transylvania in the 6th century BCE. Their origins are debated: they may have been a Scythian-influenced elite over a Thracian population, and Greek myth made their founder Agathyrsus a son of Heracles.
agathyrsi.r: Herodotus describes them as wearing much gold, tattooing themselves and holding wives in common so that all would be kin. Their king Spargapeithes killed the Scythian king Ariapeithes. When Darius I invaded Scythia around 513 BCE, they refused Scythian refugees entry to their land. Scythian-style graves in Transylvania are often linked to them.
agathyrsi.e: After the 5th century BCE they vanish from the record; their lands later appear as part of the territory of the Getae and Dacians, into whom they were probably absorbed.

ava-kingdom.t: The dominant kingdom of Upper Burma for nearly two centuries, which fought the Mon of Hanthawaddy for forty years and shaped classical Burmese literature.
ava-kingdom.o: After Shan raiders sacked Pinya and Sagaing in 1364, Thado Minbya united the two courts and in 1365 founded a new capital at Ava, Inwa, at the confluence of the Irrawaddy and Myitnge rivers. He presented his kingdom as the successor of the Pagan Kingdom.
ava-kingdom.r: Ava controlled the Kyaukse and Minbu rice lands and claimed authority over Prome, Toungoo and the Shan borders. Minkhaung I fought the Forty Years' War against Razadarit of the Hanthawaddy Kingdom from 1385 to 1424. Monks and court poets such as Shin Maha Thilawuntha and Shin Maha Rahtathara made Ava the golden age of Burmese classical literature.
ava-kingdom.e: Ava weakened as vassals broke away, including Prome and Toungoo. In 1527 a confederation of Shan states led by Mohnyin captured Ava, ruling it as the Confederation of Shan States. In 1555 Bayinnaung of the First Toungoo Empire conquered it, and Ava later became the capital of the Restored Toungoo Kingdom.

akalkot-state.t: A Bhonsle Maratha state of the Deccan, founded by the adopted son of Chhatrapati Shahu, and home of the saint Swami Samarth.
akalkot-state.o: Akkalkot was granted in 1708 to Fatehsinh Bhonsle, born into the Lokhande family and adopted as a boy by the Maratha king Shahu. His descendants ruled as Rajas under the Satara Chhatrapatis.
akalkot-state.r: The Rajas governed a dry Deccan territory of millet and cotton near Solapur. After 1818 the state came under British protection, later the Deccan States Agency. In the 19th century Akkalkot became famous as the home of the saint Swami Samarth, whose shrine draws pilgrims.
akalkot-state.e: Akkalkot merged into Bombay Province in 1948 and became part of Maharashtra in 1960, in Solapur district.

ayyubid-emirate-of-damascus.t: The Ayyubid principality of Damascus after Saladin, a prize fought over by his brothers, sons and grandsons until the Mongols arrived in 1260.
ayyubid-emirate-of-damascus.o: When Saladin died in Damascus in 1193, his empire was divided among his sons, and Damascus went to the eldest, al-Afdal Ali. In 1196 his uncle al-Adil and brother al-Aziz drove him out, and Damascus passed to al-Adil's line.
ayyubid-emirate-of-damascus.r: Damascus was the richest prize in Syria and the seat of a scholarly and religious elite. Al-Mu'azzam Isa (1218-1227), a Hanafi jurist, built schools and dismantled the walls of Jerusalem in 1219 to keep them from the Crusaders. Later princes, al-Nasir Dawud, al-Ashraf Musa and al-Salih Ismail, fought the sultans in Egypt; al-Salih Ismail even ceded castles to the Franks. Al-Salih Ayyub took the city in 1245.
ayyubid-emirate-of-damascus.e: Al-Nasir Yusuf of the Ayyubid Emirate of Aleppo seized Damascus in 1250. The Mongols occupied it in March 1260, and after their defeat at Ain Jalut it passed to the Mamluks.

arretium.t: Northern Etruscan city, home of the bronze Chimera of Arezzo, which grew rich on farming and metalworking and became an early Roman ally.
arretium.o: Arretium, Etruscan Aritim, modern Arezzo, lay where the Val di Chiana meets the upper Arno, controlling routes between Etruria, Umbria and the Po valley. It developed into a city from the 6th century BCE, later than most Etruscan centres, and grew powerful in the 4th century BCE.
arretium.r: Arretium was known for agriculture and metalwork. The bronze Chimera of Arezzo, cast around 400 BCE and found in 1553, is a masterpiece of Etruscan art. The city was dominated by great families, among them the Cilnii, whom Livy reports being driven out by a popular revolt in 302 BCE and restored with Roman help; the Augustan minister Maecenas was descended from them.
arretium.e: Arretium made truces with Rome in 310 and 294 BCE and became a loyal ally, supplying weapons and grain to Scipio in 205 BCE. Under Rome it became famous for Arretine ware, a red-glazed tableware exported across the empire. The town continued as Arezzo, birthplace of Petrarch.

afrighid-khwarazm.t: The native dynasty of Khwarazm for nearly seven centuries, whose shahs kept the region's Iranian culture alive through Arab conquest and Samanid overlordship.
afrighid-khwarazm.o: According to the Khwarazmian scholar al-Biruni, the Afrighid dynasty was founded by Afrig in 305 CE, succeeding the older royal house of the Kingdom of Khwarazm. Afrig built a fortress at Kath on the Amu Darya, which became the capital.
afrighid-khwarazm.r: The shahs ruled an irrigated land of canals, towns and fortified manors that traded north with the steppe and the Volga. Zoroastrianism and the Khwarazmian language and calendar persisted. After the Arab general Qutayba ibn Muslim conquered Khwarazm in 712, the shahs remained as vassals, converted to Islam and ruled under Caliphal and later Samanid authority, while a rival centre grew at Gurganj.
afrighid-khwarazm.e: In 995 the emir of Gurganj, Ma'mun ibn Muhammad, overthrew and killed the last Afrighid shah, Abu Abdallah Muhammad, and founded Ma'munid Khwarazm. Al-Biruni, born near Kath, preserved much of what is known of the dynasty.
