assuwa.t: Assuwa, a short-lived league of western Anatolian lands that rose against the Hittites c. 1430 BCE and may have given Asia its name.
assuwa.o: Assuwa was a coalition of 22 lands in north-western Anatolia, including Wilusiya and Taruisa, often linked with Troy. It formed in the 15th century BCE in resistance to Hittite expansion westward.
assuwa.r: Known almost only from the annals of Tudhaliya I of the Hittite Empire, the league was led by Piyama-Kurunta and his son Kukkuli. A bronze sword of Aegean type, inscribed with Tudhaliya's dedication after the victory over Assuwa, was found at Hattusa in 1991.
assuwa.e: Tudhaliya I defeated the coalition and deported thousands of soldiers and chariots. Kukkuli rebelled again and was killed. The name may survive in the Greek and Roman name Asia.

apollonia-pontica.t: Milesian colony on the Black Sea coast of Thrace whose colossal statue of Apollo was carried off to Rome in 72 BCE.
apollonia-pontica.o: Settlers from Miletus founded Apollonia c. 610 BCE on a peninsula and island on the western Black Sea coast, at modern Sozopol in Bulgaria. Named after Apollo, it became one of the leading Greek cities of the Thracian coast.
apollonia-pontica.r: Apollonia traded wine, oil and fine pottery with the Thracians, including the Odrysian Kingdom, for grain, metals and honey. Its coins carried an anchor. In the 5th century BCE it set up a bronze statue of Apollo by Calamis, about 13 metres high. It was governed as an oligarchy and later a democracy.
apollonia-pontica.e: In 72 BCE Marcus Lucullus captured Apollonia during the Third Mithridatic War and took the Apollo statue to the Capitol in Rome. The city then came under Roman control and survives as Sozopol.

alwar-state.t: A Kachhwaha Rajput state of north-eastern Rajasthan, founded by the Naruka chief Pratap Singh in breakaway from Jaipur.
alwar-state.o: Pratap Singh, a Naruka Kachhwaha noble of Jaipur, built up his own holding around Rajgarh and took the fort of Alwar in 1775, founding an independent state around 1770–75. He exploited the decline of the Jats of Bharatpur and of Mughal power.
alwar-state.r: Bakhtawar Singh allied with the British against the Marathas in 1803 and received protection. Alwar had a 15-gun salute and a Rajput ruling class over a mixed Hindu and Meo Muslim peasantry. Maharaja Jai Singh (1892–1937), a gifted but erratic ruler, was removed by the British in 1933 after a Meo uprising and misgovernment.
alwar-state.e: Tej Singh acceded to India, and in March 1948 Alwar became the capital of the Matsya Union, which joined the United State of Rajasthan in 1949.

asahan-sultanate.t: Malay sultanate on the east coast of Sumatra that grew rich from colonial plantations before its fall in the revolution of 1946.
asahan-sultanate.o: Tradition holds that Asahan was founded around 1630 by Abdul Jalil, a son of Sultan Iskandar Muda of the Aceh Sultanate by a local woman, at the mouth of the Asahan river. For two centuries it was a minor coastal state under Acehnese and later Siak overlordship, trading with its Batak hinterland.
asahan-sultanate.r: The sultan ruled from Tanjung Balai over Malay river communities and collected duties on forest products, rice and slaves brought down from the Batak highlands. Dutch control from 1865 turned Asahan into part of the plantation belt of East Sumatra, where tobacco, rubber and oil palm estates brought the court large concession revenues.
asahan-sultanate.e: The sultanate lived on as a self-governing domain of the Dutch East Indies. During the social revolution in East Sumatra in March 1946, the Malay aristocracy was attacked by revolutionary groups and the sultanate collapsed, its territory passing to the Republic of Indonesia.

ayutthaya-kingdom.t: The great Siamese kingdom on the Chao Phraya that for four centuries dominated mainland Southeast Asia's trade and welcomed merchants from Persia to Japan.
ayutthaya-kingdom.o: In 1351 U Thong, a ruler with links to Lavo and Suphannaphum, founded Ayutthaya on an island where the Lopburi, Pa Sak and Chao Phraya rivers meet, and reigned as Ramathibodi I. The site gave access to the sea and to rice lands of the central plain.
ayutthaya-kingdom.r: Ayutthaya's kings combined Theravada Buddhist kingship with Khmer-style royal ritual. Borommatrailokkanat organised government into civil and military ministries and the sakdina ranking of land and status. The capital became a cosmopolitan port with Portuguese, Dutch, Japanese, Chinese and Persian quarters; under Narai it exchanged embassies with Louis XIV. It absorbed Sukhothai, sacked Angkor in 1431 and fought long wars with Burma.
ayutthaya-kingdom.e: Bayinnaung of the First Toungoo Empire conquered Ayutthaya in 1569, but Naresuan restored independence in 1584. In 1767 Konbaung armies sacked and burned the city, ending the kingdom. Taksin rallied resistance from Thonburi, and the ruins of Ayutthaya are now a World Heritage Site.

awadh-state.t: The kingdom of the Nawabs of Awadh, whose courts at Faizabad and Lucknow were famed for refinement, until its British annexation helped spark 1857.
awadh-state.o: In 1722 the Mughal emperor Muhammad Shah appointed Saadat Ali Khan, a Shia noble from Nishapur, as governor of Awadh. As Mughal power weakened, he and his nephew Safdar Jang made the governorship hereditary, ruling the rich middle Ganges plain from Faizabad and, from 1775, Lucknow.
awadh-state.r: Shuja ud-Daula's defeat at Buxar in 1764 made Awadh a subsidiary ally of the British East India Company, which stationed troops at its expense. Asaf ud-Daula built the Bara Imambara in Lucknow, and the court patronised Urdu poetry, kathak dance, thumri music and a celebrated cuisine. Ghazi ud-Din Haidar took the title of king in 1819 with British encouragement. Shia Islam was the court religion.
awadh-state.e: Governor-General Dalhousie annexed Awadh in 1856, alleging misrule, and exiled Wajid Ali Shah to Calcutta. Resentment among Awadhi soldiers and landholders fed the 1857 rebellion, in which Begum Hazrat Mahal led resistance at Lucknow.

azerbaijan.t: The independent Republic of Azerbaijan on the Caspian Sea, an oil and gas producer whose post-Soviet history has been dominated by the Karabakh conflict.
azerbaijan.o: The Azerbaijan SSR declared independence on 30 August 1991, confirmed by a constitutional act on 18 October 1991, and became fully sovereign with the dissolution of the Soviet Union in December. It claimed descent from the Azerbaijan Democratic Republic of 1918-1920, whose flag it readopted, while war with Armenian forces over Nagorno-Karabakh was already under way.
azerbaijan.r: After defeat in the First Karabakh War and a 1994 ceasefire that left Armenian forces holding Karabakh and surrounding districts, Heydar Aliyev, president from 1993, built a strong presidential system, passed to his son Ilham Aliyev in 2003. The 1994 Contract of the Century and the Baku-Tbilisi-Ceyhan pipeline, opened in 2005, brought oil wealth and Western investment. The state is secular, with a Shia majority.
azerbaijan.e: In the 2020 war Azerbaijan regained much of the lost territory, and a 2023 offensive brought all of Karabakh under its control, prompting the flight of its Armenian population. Peace talks with Armenia continue.

anlo.t: The leading Ewe state on the coast of south-eastern Ghana, centred on Anloga by the Keta lagoon, a trading and military power until British annexation.
anlo.o: Anlo tradition traces its people to Notsie, in modern Togo, from which the Ewe escaped the tyranny of King Agokoli and dispersed, probably in the 17th century. Under their leader Sri I the Anlo settled the sandbar between the sea and the Keta lagoon and made Anloga their capital, gradually becoming the most important of the coastal Ewe states.
anlo.r: The paramount ruler, the Awoamefia, was a sacred figure who lived largely in seclusion, while war leaders and lineage heads handled daily affairs. The army was organised in three wings. Anlo traded fish, salt and slaves with Europeans at Keta, where the Danes built Fort Prinzenstein in 1784, and it fought long wars with the Ga, Ada and Akwamu. Shrine societies such as Yewe were influential.
anlo.e: British forces campaigned in the region in the 1860s and 1870s, and after the defeat of the Ashanti Empire in 1874 Anlo was annexed to the Gold Coast Colony, despite resistance into 1878. The Awoamefia remains the traditional ruler of the Anlo state.

annazid-dynasty.t: A Kurdish dynasty that controlled the Zagros passes between Iraq and Iran from its base at Hulwan for over a century.
annazid-dynasty.o: Abu'l-Fath Muhammad ibn Annaz, chief of the Kurdish Shadhanjan tribe, established himself at Hulwan on the road from Baghdad to Hamadan around 990, as Buyid authority weakened. The Annazids competed with the Hasanwayhid dynasty, taking over much of their territory after 1015.
annazid-dynasty.r: The Annazids were tribal rulers who controlled key passes, collecting tolls and tribute and playing Buyids, Kakuyids and other neighbours against each other. Abu'l-Shawk Faris extended their power to Dinavar and Kermanshah, but family feuds were frequent. Their towns included Hulwan, Dinavar and Shahrizor.
annazid-dynasty.e: The arrival of the Seljuk Empire in the 1040s brought repeated invasions, and the Annazids became Seljuk vassals. They lost their last strongholds around 1117.

astrakhan-khanate.t: A Tatar khanate at the mouth of the Volga, a successor of the Golden Horde whose annexation in 1556 gave Russia the whole Volga route.
astrakhan-khanate.o: The Astrakhan Khanate formed in the 1460s around the town of Xacitarxan near the Volga delta, under khans descended from Küchük Muhammad of the Great Horde. It became fully independent after the Great Horde's destruction in 1502.
astrakhan-khanate.r: The khanate was small and relatively weak, controlling the fisheries and trade of the lower Volga, including the caravan routes towards the Caspian and Persia. Its population of Tatars and Nogais lived largely by herding and trade. Its khans were frequently dependent on the Nogai Horde or the Crimean Khanate, and several were installed by these neighbours.
astrakhan-khanate.e: After taking Kazan, Ivan IV turned south: Russian forces installed a client khan, Dervish Ali, in 1554 and annexed the khanate in 1556. Astrakhan became a Russian fortress city and gateway to the Caspian and the Caucasus.

ayyubid-emirate-of-aleppo.t: The Ayyubid principality of northern Syria whose rulers built much of the Citadel of Aleppo as it stands today.
ayyubid-emirate-of-aleppo.o: Saladin took Aleppo from the Zengids in 1183 and in 1186 gave it to his son al-Zahir Ghazi, whose line ruled it until the Mongol invasion.
ayyubid-emirate-of-aleppo.r: Al-Zahir Ghazi rebuilt the Citadel of Aleppo with its sloping glacis, monumental gate and water supply, and endowed madrasas. His widow Dayfa Khatun, a niece of Saladin, governed as regent from 1236 to 1242, one of the few women to rule in medieval Syria, and founded the Firdaws madrasa. Aleppo kept treaties with Venice and the Principality of Antioch and flourished on trade. Al-Nasir Yusuf took Damascus in 1250, ruling most of Syria.
ayyubid-emirate-of-aleppo.e: Hulagu's Mongols stormed Aleppo in January 1260 and massacred many inhabitants. Al-Nasir Yusuf fled, was captured and was later killed by the Mongols. After Ain Jalut, Aleppo passed to the Mamluks.

aksumite-yemen.t: Yemen under Ethiopian Christian rule, best known for Abraha, who repaired the Marib Dam and, by tradition, marched on Mecca with an elephant.
aksumite-yemen.o: In 525 the Aksumite Empire under King Kaleb crossed the Red Sea to avenge the Christians of Najran, defeated the Himyarite king Yusuf and installed Sumyafa Ashwa, a local Christian, as viceroy. Within a few years the Aksumite general Abraha overthrew him and made himself ruler, nominally under Aksum.
aksumite-yemen.r: Abraha governed in practice independently from Sanaa. His inscriptions record the restoration of the Marib Dam in 548 and a diplomatic conference attended by envoys of the Byzantine Empire, Persia and the Arab kings. He built a great church in Sanaa and campaigned deep into central Arabia; Muslim tradition remembers his failed expedition against Mecca in the Year of the Elephant.
aksumite-yemen.e: Abraha's sons Yaksum and Masruq were unpopular. The Himyarite noble Sayf ibn Dhi Yazan sought help from Persia, and around 570 a Sasanian force under Wahriz defeated the Ethiopians, opening the period of Sasanian Yemen.

aq-qoyunlu.t: The 'White Sheep' Turkmen confederation that rose from Diyarbakir to rule Iran under Uzun Hasan before giving way to the Safavids.
aq-qoyunlu.o: The Aq Qoyunlu were led by the Bayandur clan among the Turkmen tribes pasturing around Diyarbakir in the late 14th century. Their chief Qara Yuluk Osman fought the Kadi Burhan al-Din state and the Qara Qoyunlu, sided with Timur, and was rewarded with Diyarbakir.
aq-qoyunlu.r: Uzun Hasan defeated the Qara Qoyunlu ruler Jahan Shah in 1467 and the Timurid Abu Sa'id in 1469, making Tabriz his capital and ruling Iran, Iraq and eastern Anatolia. He allied with Venice against the Ottomans, but Mehmed II defeated him at Otlukbeli in 1473. His son Ya'qub kept a Persianate court that patronised poets and painters, while tribal chiefs held real military power.
aq-qoyunlu.e: After Ya'qub's death in 1490 the confederation split among rival princes. Ismail, grandson of Uzun Hasan through his daughter, defeated them in 1501 and founded the Safavid state; the last Aq Qoyunlu ruler, Murad, was driven out in 1503.

africa-proconsularis.t: Rome's richest African province, centred on rebuilt Carthage, the granary of Rome and a heartland of Latin Christianity.
africa-proconsularis.o: After destroying Carthage in 146 BCE, the Roman Republic made its territory the province of Africa, governed from Utica. In 46 BCE Caesar added Numidian lands as Africa Nova, and under Augustus the two were joined as Africa Proconsularis, governed by a senatorial proconsul. Carthage was refounded as a Roman colony and became the capital.
africa-proconsularis.r: The province supplied much of Rome's grain and, later, olive oil and fine red pottery, and its cities, such as Thugga, Thysdrus and Leptis Magna, were full of temples, baths and amphitheatres. Punic and Berber survived beside Latin. In 238 a revolt at Thysdrus proclaimed the governor Gordian I emperor. Africa became a centre of Latin Christianity, home of Tertullian and Cyprian, and was divided by the Donatist schism.
africa-proconsularis.e: Diocletian split the province around 303, creating Byzacena and Tripolitania. The Vandals, who had crossed from Spain in 429, took Carthage in 439, founding the Vandal Kingdom. Justinian's reconquest restored Roman rule in 534.

appenzell-ausserrhoden.t: The Reformed half of Appenzell, created in 1597, which became one of the most industrialised rural areas of early modern Europe.
appenzell-ausserrhoden.o: When the Canton of Appenzell was divided in 1597, the outer districts, which had adopted the Reformed faith, formed Ausserrhoden. Without the old capital, its Landsgemeinde met alternately in Trogen and Hundwil, and government business was shared between Trogen and Herisau.
appenzell-ausserrhoden.r: From the 17th century the villagers spun and wove linen and later cotton at home, and merchant families such as the Zellwegers of Trogen grew rich in international trade. Government lay with the Landsgemeinde and councils, and the half-canton shared a vote with Innerrhoden at the federal Diet.
appenzell-ausserrhoden.e: In 1798 it was absorbed into the canton of Säntis of the Helvetic Republic, and in 1803 it was restored as a half-canton. Ausserrhoden abolished its Landsgemeinde in 1997 and remains a Swiss canton.

azzi-hayasa.t: Azzi-Hayasa, a mountain confederation of north-eastern Anatolia that fought the Hittites in the 14th century BCE.
azzi-hayasa.o: Hayasa and Azzi were lands in the highlands of the upper Euphrates and the Erzurum region. They appear in Hittite records from the 15th century BCE as a federation of mountain communities beyond the Hittite frontier.
azzi-hayasa.r: Little is known of its internal structure. Suppiluliuma I of the Hittite Empire made a treaty with Hukkana of Hayasa and gave him his sister in marriage, with strict rules about Hittite customs. Some scholars connect Hayasa with the Armenian name for Armenia, Hay, though this is disputed.
azzi-hayasa.e: Mursili II fought Anniya of Azzi in long campaigns, and Hayasa disappears from the record in the 13th century BCE. The highlands later formed part of Nairi and the Kingdom of Urartu.

austrian-delagoa-bay.t: The Habsburg monarchy's only African colony, a brief trading venture on Delagoa Bay led by the adventurer William Bolts.
austrian-delagoa-bay.o: William Bolts, a former East India Company servant, persuaded the Austrian government of Maria Theresa to back a trading venture to the East under the imperial flag. In 1777 he landed at Delagoa Bay and signed agreements with local Tsonga rulers, including the Tembe Kingdom, to establish trading posts.
austrian-delagoa-bay.r: The Austrian posts, run by agents of Bolts's company and later the Imperial Asiatic Company of Trieste, traded cloth and metal goods for ivory. The settlement was tiny and dependent on the goodwill of local rulers, and it was meant to link Austrian trade with India and China.
austrian-delagoa-bay.e: Portugal, which claimed the bay, sent a naval force in 1781 that expelled the Austrians and built a fort. Bolts's company soon failed, and Austria made no further colonial attempts in Africa.

alodia.t: The southernmost Christian kingdom of Nubia, centred on Soba near modern Khartoum, which lasted for nearly a thousand years.
alodia.o: Alodia (Alwa) arose by around 500 in the region of the Blue and White Niles and the Butana plain, once the heartland of the Kushite Empire of Meroë. Its capital was Soba, on the Blue Nile. Around 580 the Miaphysite bishop Longinus, who had earlier converted Nobadia, brought Christianity to the court.
alodia.r: Alodia was the largest of the Nubian kingdoms, with farmland, cattle and trade routes to the Red Sea and Ethiopia. The 10th-century Egyptian writer Ibn Sulaym al-Aswani described it as richer and more populous than Makuria, with many churches at Soba and a ruler governing through subordinate kings. Soba's excavated churches and imported glass and pottery confirm its wealth.
alodia.e: From the 12th century Alodia declined, losing territory to Arab nomads. Around 1504 Soba fell to an alliance of the Abdallab Arabs and the Funj, founding the Funj Sultanate. Christianity faded, though memories of Soba lived on in Sudanese tradition.

acarnanian-league.t: Federation of the Acarnanian towns of western Greece, a long-standing enemy of the Aetolians and an ally first of Athens and later of Macedon.
acarnanian-league.o: Acarnania, between the Ambracian Gulf and the Achelous river, was a land of small towns and villages. By the mid-5th century BCE they were acting together as a league with its meeting place at Stratos. Hostility to Corinth's colonies in the region pushed them into alliance with Athens, whose general Phormio campaigned with them in the Peloponnesian War.
acarnanian-league.r: The league had a federal assembly, council and elected general (strategos), and struck federal coins. Its members were mainly farmers and herders known as skilled slingers and fighters. Ancient writers considered the Acarnanians conservative and fiercely loyal to allies, especially in their long struggle against the expanding Aetolian League.
acarnanian-league.e: Aetolia and Epirus partitioned Acarnania in the mid-3rd century BCE, but the league was restored around 230 BCE and sided with Macedon. Rome detached Leucas and made it the federal capital in 197 BCE. The league faded under Roman rule; after Actium in 31 BCE Augustus moved much of its population to his new city of Nicopolis.

albanian-kingdom-1943-1944.t: Nominally independent Albanian state set up by Germany after Italy's surrender in 1943, which kept Kosovo but was defeated by the Communist Partisans.
albanian-kingdom-1943-1944.o: When Italy capitulated in September 1943, German troops occupied the Albanian Kingdom (1939-1943). Seeking local support, Germany declared Albania independent, convened a national assembly and set up a Regency Council headed by Mehdi Frashëri, with Albanian governments led successively by figures such as Rexhep Mitrovica.
albanian-kingdom-1943-1944.r: The regime claimed neutrality and kept the Albanian-inhabited lands of Kosovo and western Macedonia added in 1941, while Germany controlled the military situation. Some nationalists of the Balli Kombëtar cooperated with the Germans against the Partisans, and an SS division was recruited in Kosovo. Many Jews in Albania were sheltered by Albanian families and survived.
albanian-kingdom-1943-1944.e: Enver Hoxha's Partisans won the civil war and took Tirana on 17 November 1944 as German forces withdrew. The communists then founded what became the People's Socialist Republic of Albania, and Kosovo returned to Yugoslavia.
albanian-kingdom-1943-1944.re: Sunni Islam, Orthodox and Catholic Christianity

akatziri.t: A steppe people north of the Black Sea who were drawn into Attila's empire and later appear among the forerunners of the Khazars.
akatziri.o: The Akatziri are first mentioned by the Byzantine envoy Priscus in the 440s as a people of the Pontic steppe ruled by many chiefs. Jordanes later described them as a strong people who lived by herding and hunting. Their origins and language are unknown; they were probably a Hunnic or early Turkic group.
akatziri.r: Around 448 the Eastern Roman emperor Theodosius II tried to bribe their chiefs to turn against Attila, but the gifts went to the wrong chief, Kuridachus, who betrayed the plan. Attila then subdued them and set his eldest son Ellac over them as king, bringing them firmly into the Hunnic Empire.
akatziri.e: After the collapse of Hun power in the 450s and 460s, the Akatziri disappear from the record, displaced or absorbed by the Saragurs, Sabirs and Onogurs. Some historians link them to the later Khazars, though the connection is unproven.

aqrabi-sheikhdom.t: A tiny sheikhdom west of Aden whose land included the peninsula where Britain built the Little Aden oil refinery.
aqrabi-sheikhdom.o: The Aqrabi tribe held a small coastal district west of Aden, with its seat at Bir Ahmad. They broke from the neighbouring Sultanate of Lahej in the 18th century to form their own sheikhdom. Its early history is poorly known.
aqrabi-sheikhdom.r: With only a few thousand inhabitants, the sheikhdom lived from farming, fishing and its position near Aden. In the 1860s Britain bought the Little Aden peninsula from the Aqrabi sheikh, and it became part of British Aden; a large oil refinery opened there in 1954. The sheikhdom was a British-protected state and joined the Federation of South Arabia.
aqrabi-sheikhdom.e: In 1967 the National Liberation Front took over, and the territory was incorporated into South Yemen.

anuradhapura-kingdom.t: Sri Lanka's longest-lived kingdom, where Theravada Buddhism took root and kings built vast irrigation tanks and giant stupas over 1,400 years.
anuradhapura-kingdom.o: The chronicles say King Pandukabhaya founded Anuradhapura around 437 BCE, succeeding the Kingdom of Tambapanni. In the 3rd century BCE, under Devanampiya Tissa, the monk Mahinda, son of the Maurya emperor Ashoka, brought Buddhism, and a sapling of the Bodhi tree was planted in the city. Around 161 BCE Dutugemunu defeated the Tamil ruler Elara and united the island.
anuradhapura-kingdom.r: Kings ruled with close ties to the Buddhist sangha; the Mahavihara and Abhayagiri monasteries were rival centres of learning, and the Pali Canon was first written down in the 1st century BCE. Huge stupas such as the Ruwanwelisaya and Jetavanaramaya rose in the capital. Rice farming depended on great reservoirs like Kala Wewa, built by Dhatusena, and ports traded with India, Rome and China.
anuradhapura-kingdom.e: Repeated invasions from South India weakened the kingdom. The Chola Empire under Rajaraja I took Anuradhapura in 993, and in 1017 Rajendra I captured King Mahinda V. The Sinhalese capital later moved to Polonnaruwa, beginning the Polonnaruwa Kingdom.

aizu-domain.t: The Tokugawa branch domain in northern Japan whose loyalty to the shogunate ended in the tragic siege of Wakamatsu castle in 1868.
aizu-domain.o: After the Uesugi were moved to Yonezawa in 1601, Aizu passed to Gamo Hideyuki and then to Kato Yoshiaki. In 1643 the shogunate gave it to Hoshina Masayuki, half-brother of Shogun Tokugawa Iemitsu, with 230,000 koku; his descendants, later surnamed Matsudaira, held it until the end.
aizu-domain.r: Masayuki's house code bound his heirs to absolute loyalty to the shogun. Aizu was known for strict samurai education at the Nisshinkan school, and for lacquerware and sake. In 1862 Matsudaira Katamori became Kyoto protector, policing the capital with the Shinsengumi and fighting Choshu radicals.
aizu-domain.e: Branded an enemy after 1868, Aizu was the target of the imperial army; the Ouetsu Reppan Domei formed partly to defend it. Wakamatsu castle fell after a month-long siege, during which young Byakkotai soldiers took their own lives. The clan was exiled to Tonami in the far north.

aruba.t: Island off Venezuela that left the Netherlands Antilles in 1986 to become a separate country within the Kingdom of the Netherlands.
aruba.o: Arubans had long resented domination by Curaçao within the Colony of Curaçao and the Netherlands Antilles. Led by Gilberto 'Betico' Croes and his People's Electoral Movement, they won a referendum for separation in 1977, and on 1 January 1986 Aruba gained 'status aparte' as an autonomous country in the kingdom, with independence planned for 1996.
aruba.r: Aruba has its own parliament, prime minister, constitution and currency, the florin, while the Netherlands manages defence and foreign affairs and a governor represents the monarch. The closure of the Lago oil refinery in 1985 forced a rapid turn to tourism, which now dominates. Papiamento and Dutch are official languages. Henny Eman became the first prime minister, followed by leaders such as Nelson Oduber and Evelyn Wever-Croes.
aruba.e: In 1990 Aruba asked to postpone independence, and in 1995 the plan was dropped, leaving it a permanent country within the kingdom. It remains among the most prosperous Caribbean islands, though heavily dependent on American tourism.

achaemenid-egypt.t: Egypt as a satrapy of the Persian Empire, ruled by Persian kings who were also crowned as pharaohs.
achaemenid-egypt.o: In 525 BCE Cambyses II defeated Psamtik III of the Twenty-sixth Dynasty of Egypt at Pelusium and took Memphis, making Egypt a province of the Achaemenid Empire. Manetho counts the Persian kings as the Twenty-seventh Dynasty. The Egyptian official Udjahorresnet helped Cambyses adopt pharaonic titles.
achaemenid-egypt.r: A Persian satrap governed from Memphis, collecting tribute in grain and silver. Darius I had Egyptian laws collected, completed the Nile to Red Sea canal and built the temple of Hibis in the Kharga Oasis. Aramaic served as the administrative language beside Egyptian, and a garrison of Jewish soldiers at Elephantine left a rich archive of Aramaic papyri. Revolts broke out in 486 BCE and under Inaros, who was supported by Athens, around 460 BCE.
achaemenid-egypt.e: After the death of Darius II, the Saite noble Amyrtaeus rebelled in 404 BCE and freed Egypt, founding the Twenty-eighth Dynasty of Egypt. Persia reconquered the country in 343 BCE.

akuapem.t: A small Akan and Guan state on the Akuapem ridge north of Accra, formed after the fall of Akwamu and later a centre of Basel Mission Christianity and Twi literacy.
akuapem.o: The Akuapem ridge was home to Guan-speaking towns that had been subject to Akwamu. In 1733, after Akyem Abuakwa and its allies broke Akwamu power, the ridge towns accepted an Akyem leader, Safori, as their ruler. He became the first Okuapehene, with his capital at Akropong, and the new state joined Guan and Akan communities under one paramount chief.
akuapem.r: Akuapem followed Akan political forms, with a paramount chief, divisional chiefs and the Odwira festival, while Guan towns kept their own traditions. Farmers on the ridge later led the expansion of cocoa growing in the Gold Coast. The Basel Mission settled at Akropong in 1835, and missionaries such as Johann Christaller made Akuapem Twi the basis of a written Twi language and Bible.
akuapem.e: Akuapem came under British protection and was absorbed into the Gold Coast Colony in 1874. The Okuapehene still reigns at Akropong, and the town remains an important educational and church centre in Ghana.

aowin.t: A gold-producing Akan kingdom of the Anyi people on the forest frontier of modern Ghana and Ivory Coast, best remembered for raiding Kumasi before its defeat by the Ashanti Empire.
aowin.o: Aowin took shape in the 17th century in the forested country west of the Tano river, settled by Anyi-speaking Akan groups who had migrated from the north and east. Its rise belongs to the same period of gold-fuelled state building that produced Denkyira and Akwamu, and it held land along the trade paths that ran from the goldfields towards the coast.
aowin.r: Little is documented about its institutions, which are known mainly from Akan oral tradition and scattered European notes. Like its neighbours it was ruled by a king from a royal matrilineage, supported by chiefs of subordinate towns. Its wealth came from alluvial and mined gold and from the slaves and ivory carried to coastal forts. Religion was the Akan worship of a creator god, lesser deities and ancestors.
aowin.e: In the early 18th century Aowin forces under Ebiri Moro raided Kumasi, but the Ashanti Empire retaliated and overran the kingdom. Many Aowin moved west and south, where their descendants founded or strengthened the Anyi states of the lagoon country, notably the Kingdom of Sanwi at Krinjabo.

aulerci-cenomani.t: Gallic people of Maine, centred on Le Mans, a branch of whom crossed the Alps and founded the Celtic towns of Brescia and Verona.
aulerci-cenomani.o: The Cenomani were the largest branch of the Aulerci and held the Sarthe valley around Vindinum (Le Mans). Livy and Polybius report that part of the people migrated across the Alps around 400 BCE and settled north of the Po, where the Italian Cenomani founded Brixia (Brescia) and became allies of Rome against the other Gauls.
aulerci-cenomani.r: Little is known of the Gallic Cenomani at home. They struck gold coins and controlled the route between the Loire and the Channel coast.
aulerci-cenomani.e: They joined the great revolt of 52 BCE and sent five thousand men to relieve Alesia. Under Rome Vindinum grew into a walled town, later called Civitas Cenomanorum, from which come the names Le Mans and Maine.

antigonid-kingdom-of-macedonia.t: Kingdom of the Antigonid dynasty, which ruled Macedon and dominated Greece for over a century until defeated by Rome at Pydna in 168 BCE.
antigonid-kingdom-of-macedonia.o: Antigonus I Monophthalmus and his son Demetrius Poliorcetes, generals of Alexander, took the royal title in 306 BCE while ruling in Asia. Demetrius seized Macedon in 294 BCE but lost it in 288 BCE. His son Antigonus II Gonatas won the throne after defeating the Gauls at Lysimachia in 277 BCE, founding a stable dynasty at Pella.
antigonid-kingdom-of-macedonia.r: Antigonid kings ruled Macedon directly through a landed aristocracy and a citizen army famous for its sarissa phalanx, while controlling Greece through garrisons at Corinth, Chalcis and Demetrias, the 'fetters of Greece'. They patronised philosophy and the arts. Antigonus III Doson formed a Hellenic alliance and defeated Sparta at Sellasia in 222 BCE.
antigonid-kingdom-of-macedonia.e: Philip V's alliance with Hannibal led to wars with Rome; defeat at Cynoscephalae in 197 BCE confined him to Macedon. His son Perseus lost to Lucius Aemilius Paullus at Pydna in 168 BCE. Rome abolished the monarchy and divided the land into the Four Macedonian Republics.

aurunci.t: Ancient Italic people of the coast between Latium and Campania, whose towns were destroyed by Rome in 314 BCE.
aurunci.o: The Aurunci, called Ausones by the Greeks, lived between the Liri and Volturno rivers around the Roccamonfina volcano. Greek writers used 'Ausonia' for much of early Italy, which suggests they were once a widespread people. Little is known of their origins or language.
aurunci.r: Known only from Roman and Greek sources, the Aurunci lived in hill towns such as Ausona, Minturnae, Vescia and Suessa Aurunca. They fought Rome and the Latins in the 6th and 5th centuries BCE, and later allied with the Sidicini against the Samnites.
aurunci.e: After they joined Rome's enemies during the Samnite Wars, Rome destroyed the towns of Ausona, Minturnae and Vescia in 314 BCE, massacring much of the population. Roman colonies followed at Suessa Aurunca in 313 BCE and Minturnae in 296 BCE, and the people disappeared from history.

acco.t: Acco, a Canaanite harbour town on the bay of Haifa, a vassal of Egypt in the Amarna age and forerunner of the later port of Acre.
acco.o: Akka grew on Tel Akko, beside the mouth of the Na'aman river, in the Middle Bronze Age, when it was surrounded by massive earth ramparts. It is named in Egyptian execration texts and in the list of towns conquered by Thutmose III.
acco.r: As a vassal of the Egyptian Empire New Kingdom it was governed by local kings who traded with Cyprus and the Aegean through its harbour. Its rulers Zurata and Zatatna appear in the Amarna letters, accused by neighbours of plotting with Egypt's enemies.
acco.e: Acco's Canaanite kingdom ended in the upheavals of the 12th century BCE. The city later came under Phoenician rule, was renamed Ptolemais by the Ptolemaic Empire, and survives as Acre.

aceh-sultanate.t: The powerful Muslim sultanate of northern Sumatra, rival of Portuguese Malacca, centre of Islamic scholarship, and fierce opponent of the Dutch.
aceh-sultanate.o: Aceh grew from a small port near the old Lamuri kingdom. Sultan Ali Mughayat Syah, ruling from about 1514, united the north of Sumatra, conquering Pedir in 1524 and expelling the Portuguese from Samudera Pasai. His capital, later called Kutaraja and now Banda Aceh, controlled the northern entrance to the Strait of Malacca.
aceh-sultanate.r: Aceh dominated the pepper trade and sought Ottoman help against the Portuguese in the 1560s. Under Iskandar Muda, 1607 to 1636, it conquered much of Sumatra and the peninsula but failed to take Malacca in 1629. Scholars such as Hamzah Fansuri and Abdurrauf of Singkil wrote major Malay religious works, and four queens ruled from 1641 to 1699.
aceh-sultanate.e: The Dutch invaded in 1873, beginning the Aceh War, one of the longest colonial conflicts. Sultan Muhammad Daud Syah surrendered in 1903, though resistance continued for years. Aceh's independent past fed later movements for autonomy within Indonesia.

abdera.t: Thracian coastal city refounded by refugees from Teos, birthplace of the philosophers Democritus and Protagoras.
abdera.o: A first settlement at Abdera by Clazomenae c. 654 BCE was driven out by Thracians. Around 545 BCE citizens of Teos, fleeing the Persian general Harpagus, refounded the city on the Thracian coast east of the Nestos river.
abdera.r: Abdera grew rich from trade with the Thracian interior, minting silver coins with a griffin, and paid one of the highest tributes in the Delian League. It produced Democritus, founder of atomism, and the sophist Protagoras. Despite them, Abderites were the butt of Greek jokes about stupidity. The city was later under the influence of the Odrysian Kingdom.
abdera.e: Abdera was weakened by Thracian attacks in the 4th century BCE and annexed by Philip II of the Kingdom of Macedon c. 350 BCE. It survived under Macedonian, Ptolemaic and Roman rule as a smaller town.

arguin.t: Portugal's first fortified trading post in Africa south of the Sahara, set up in 1445 on a small island off the Mauritanian coast.
arguin.o: Portuguese expeditions sponsored by Prince Henry the Navigator reached the Bay of Arguin in 1443. In 1445 a trading post was established on the island, and a fort was built around 1455, the first permanent European factory on the West African coast.
arguin.r: Arguin traded horses, cloth and grain to Saharan traders for gold, slaves and gum arabic, diverting part of the caravan trade to the sea. It was run by a royal monopoly and a garrison, with a chapel and a small community of traders, and Berber and Sanhaja merchants came to the island to deal.
arguin.e: The Dutch took Arguin in 1633, and it then passed back and forth between the Dutch, English, French and the Brandenburger Gold Coast company, which held it from 1685. France took control in 1721. The fort was later abandoned, and the bay is now part of Mauritania's Banc d'Arguin National Park.

awan-dynasty.t: The first known royal house of Elam, which fought and treated with the kings of Akkad and whose last king briefly ruled Susa and the Diyala region.
awan-dynasty.o: Awan was a highland district of western Iran, probably north of Susa near modern Dezful or in Luristan, whose exact site is unknown. An Elamite king list from Susa names twelve kings of Awan, and the Sumerian King List says kingship passed briefly to Awan, reflecting its power in the 24th century BCE.
awan-dynasty.r: Kings of Awan led a coalition of Elamite lands and resisted the Akkadian Empire: Sargon and Rimush record victories over Elam and its allies. Naram-Sin later concluded a treaty, written in Elamite, with a ruler of Awan, probably Hita. The gods Inshushinak and Humban were central to Elamite religion. The last king, Puzur-Inshushinak, built at Susa and left inscriptions in Akkadian and in Linear Elamite, a script largely deciphered only in 2020.
awan-dynasty.e: After Akkad's collapse Puzur-Inshushinak expanded as far as Eshnunna, but he was driven back by Ur-Nammu around 2100 BCE. The Neo-Sumerian Empire took Susa, and leadership in Elam passed to the Shimashki dynasty and the wider Elamite Confederation.

apum.t: Apum, a north Mesopotamian kingdom ruling from Shamshi-Adad's former capital Shubat-Enlil, until Babylon destroyed it in 1728 BCE.
apum.o: Shubat-Enlil, at Tell Leilan in the Khabur plains, was the old city of Shehna, renamed by Shamshi-Adad as the capital of his Kingdom of Upper Mesopotamia. After his death in the 1770s BCE his realm broke apart, and the city became the seat of the local kingdom of Apum.
apum.r: Its kings, such as Haya-abum and Till-Abnu, played the great powers against each other, and their palace archives at Tell Leilan preserve letters and treaties with Assur and other neighbours. The kingdom depended on rain-fed barley farming and the trade routes across the Khabur.
apum.e: The Babylonian Empire under Samsu-iluna, Hammurabi's son, sacked Shubat-Enlil in 1728 BCE and ended the kingdom. The city was abandoned, and excavations by Yale University from 1979 recovered its archives.

alavid-dynasty.t: A Zaydi Shia state on the Caspian coast whose imams converted the Daylamites to Islam and opened the way for Daylamite power across Iran.
alavid-dynasty.o: In 864 the people of Ruyan and Tabaristan, angered by land seizures under Tahirid governors, invited Hasan ibn Zayd, a descendant of the Prophet's grandson Hasan, to lead them. With Daylamite support he took Amol and established a Zaydi imamate, calling himself al-Da'i ila'l-Haqq, 'the summoner to the truth'.
alavid-dynasty.r: The Alavids ruled in the name of a religious mission rather than the Abbasid Caliphate, governing from Amol with the help of Daylamite and Gilite warriors. Hasan ibn Zayd was succeeded by his brother Muhammad ibn Zayd, killed by the Samanids in 900. Hasan al-Utrush, known as al-Nasir al-Kabir, restored the state in 914 and converted many Daylamites and Gilites to Zaydi Islam, writing works of law still respected by Zaydis.
alavid-dynasty.e: After al-Utrush's death in 917 the dynasty became a tool of Daylamite commanders such as Makan ibn Kaki and Mardavij, and it ended around 928. Its converts went on to found the Ziyarid dynasty and Buyid dynasty.
